utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, thank you for returning to continue your evidence. There's no need, of course, to take any formal oath or anything of that sort. You took one earlier. There are three hours left of cross-examination of the accused. We will, of course, have the usual breaks. If at any time you would like to have a brief, do say so, a brief pause, of course just mention it, but we would normally have the first break in about an hour and a half. There will be three hours, as I say, ordered for his cross-examination. There will then be, I trust fairly limited, some questions from the amicus and also from the Prosecution, but we have, we understood, to take this position, that one way or another the evidence will finish today. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, please? Is it permissible or customary? I owe you an answer to your question and your request regarding where and with whom and how Mr. Milosevic established control over individual people and thus changed their opinion. I thought this question over, though I don't have any original documents with me, but on the basis of my notes and my own memories, I remembered certain instances which I wish to convey to you. The first case is that of Mr. Ivan Stambolic. When the time came for Mr. Ivan Stambolic to be re-elected to his position, Mr. Milosevic spoke to me to the effect that Stambolic should not be proposed for re-election. I discussed the matter with my associates in the government who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the first place with Aco Mitrovic and with Gacic as well. Both of them were of the opinion that Ivan Stambolic was doing so well in his new position that people in the economy, businessmen, have a lot of respect for him and felt that he was doing a very good job. After Mr. Milosevic had spoken to these people and sent a letter to the Federal Executive Council, that is the government, saying that Ivan Stambolic should not be re-elected and that Serbia did not agree with such a suggestion - and this letter was signed by Mr. Milosevic - then both these gentlemen changed their opinion, and both of them started persuading me that we should not allow Ivan Stambolic to be re-elected general manager of the Yugoslav Bank for Reconstruction and Development. In spite of this and in spite of the pressure they made and despite the fact that Ivan Gacic was the person who, at the 8th session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia had supported Ivan Stambolic and as a result has lost his position as Secretary-General of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, regardless, therefore, of the fact that he was a very close friend and associate of Ivan Stambolic, he felt that he should vote against his re-election to the position of general manager of the Yugoslav Bank for International Economic Cooperation. These are the examples that I could recollect. There are others, but perhaps not so convincing that I would be able to explain for you. There's something else that I wanted to add. Mr. Milosevic, as he himself said, came with some old documents from my former office which say and which testify to all the things that I had done during the three years that I was in Belgrade, and he said with satisfaction, "Where did we meet? Let Mr. Markovic tell us." I looked through my notes, and fortunately I managed to find a note saying that we did meet when I had said. I said that it was three or four weeks prior to my departure from Belgrade. I left Belgrade on the 21st of December, and the meeting with Milosevic was on the 21st of November. So that is quite in conformity with what I had said, three or four weeks. Something else that I managed to establish was that there had been another meeting prior to that, that is about a month prior to this meeting, and it had to do with the bombing of the Banski Dvori where Mr. Tudjman, Mesic, and I were. I forgot to mention this in the investigation or in the interview. Mr. Milosevic can check this out as he has the documents. I don't have them. It doesn't say what we discussed, but at least it says when it is that we met. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May. I hope that the time used by Mr. Markovic for his explanations will be subtracted from the time planned for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time begins now. So let us get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say, however, that this fact about a meeting between you and me on the 21st of November, you didn't see that in the review of your duties but that you found this in some notes you had.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the review of your duties, in the schedule, this meeting is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please look and see whether this meeting took place in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was the year 1991, and this is a schedule of your obligations. I don't have that on me any more. I've handed it over. Unfortunately, I didn't make a photocopy, but that doesn't change things. It is quite clear that towards the end of the year, we did not meet.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear that we did meet, and this can be checked from that document. I don't know. The Court has it or the Prosecutor. That can easily be verified that this meeting took place in my office on the 21st of November, which is four weeks prior to my departure from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you come to see me or did I come to see you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I came to see you, and I think I stayed for about two and a half to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But that again is different from what you said before, because you say -- you've said that you had come to see me prior to your departure. In fact, you now say it was a month prior to your departure?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my statement. In my statement I said that I came to see you three or four weeks prior to leaving Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue where we broke off last time. In that brief cross-examination, we covered the facts regarding your responsibility for the war in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the stenographic notes that we reviewed previously, that is the session of the 21st of August, beginning at 11.00 in 1991, the first page ends with 082, ERN number 082. I received it from the opposite side, and these stenographic notes clearly show Mr. Markovic's responsibilities for the war in Slovenia, and could it be tendered into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say anything in that connection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let's get this document. We'll find it. Mr. Nice, perhaps you can assist us on that matter. It doesn't appear to have been a document provided already. Yes. We'll get a copy from the accused and see what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you this copy now. This is the copy that I received from the opposite side. You can get it from them, because I wanted to refer to it again in continuation of my cross-examination with reference to the war in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may not be able to provide it immediately. I will do my best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give us the date again, Mr. Milosevic, and give us the details of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a session of the Presidency, which was expanded in composition, attended by us from the republics, held on the 21st of August, 1991, and these are stenographic notes, and the first page has the ERN number 00526082. That is the first page, the ERN on the first page. And the last page ends with numbers 204. That is the document that we reviewed last time. I wish to remind you that on the page with the number 244 of these minutes, 00526137, the president of Slovenia at the time, Milan Kucan, says in response to Mr. Markovic: "I don't need to persuade you that you will not find anyone in Slovenia, including these two, that is members of the federal government who will return to the Federal Executive Council and work there." SIV, S-I-V, which means the Federal Executive Council. It is a SIV which is known in Slovenia to have started the war in Slovenia. So that is what we quoted. And why, in addition to other excerpts that I don't have time to go into now because we covered them, but this is the reason why I wish to tender this document into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's deal with one thing at a time. Let's deal with the Prosecution. Do you think you can find that in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can certainly find it. It won't take very long, and we'll make it available and have it produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, if you're going to ask Mr. Markovic any questions, he must have the opportunity of seeing what the document is. Now, the most sensible course - and it may be well that it will be exhibited - the most sensible course may well be to find this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find some page numbers the accused referred to are matching with the page numbers of Exhibit 427, tab 6, but if the Prosecution can check it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that, and it may well be that we will admit it, but we need first of all to check it. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Markovic. If you want to add something, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Mr. Milosevic extracted a segment from the evolution of relations. Relations from the beginning when I joined the federal government between Slovenia and Serbia, or Serbia and Slovenia, and also between Milosevic and Kucan were extremely tense. In the final analysis, Serbia blocked all goods that were due to come from Bosnia to Serbia long before the war. All economic relations were suspended. Serbia also organised - and that means Milosevic - the visit of a large group of people, most of them highly radical, to go to Bosnia and to organise a rally there, a popular rally, and Slovenia prevented this. There was constant conflict over the problem of Kosovo and what was going on in Kosovo, so that in that context, if you review events and the war in Slovenia, it becomes quite clear that this was only a marginal aspect of what had happened until then as well as what happened after that when the decision was taken to pull out the army from Slovenia, and who took that decision and who immediately agreed with that decision prior to that. And it is absolutely not true that the Federal Executive Council took such a decision. I'm speaking from memory as I don't have the document now. It says clearly that the federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs would organise supervision over those facilities in Slovenia which were in their possession and that to do so they would use units which the army has deployed along the border, border units. The soldiers that were in Slovenia in the so-called Slovenian war, were not in the border barracks but soldiers that came out of their barracks with tanks and cannon. Therefore, someone else had taken the decision to use military force to pull them out of the barracks under full military gear. Such a decision was not taken by the Federal Executive Council nor could it have been taken by it, because if it could, then the federal Presidency would not have tortured itself and had endless meetings over the possibility of using the army. Such permission was never granted. And that is why it was felt that the Presidency was incapable of functioning in such a situation, and that is why efforts were made to topple the Presidency, and even through me to disband that Presidency and to use me to carry out a kind of state coup as proposed by Kadijevic. So what Milosevic is now saying is not right, because when the decision was to be taken to withdraw the army from Slovenia, that decision was in fact taken by the army, Milosevic, and Kucan. The rest of us -- I had no right to vote at the Presidency, but other members of the Presidency were also extremely concerned over what was happening, and from there the army was transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have to make myself quite clear: I was against the withdrawal of the army. I wanted it to continue to be dispersed throughout the country because it would have less opportunity of committing aggression if it is not concentrated in one place, but this was not in my hands. I couldn't take any such decision. Nowhere is there any possibility envisaged for the federal government to have command over the army. It was only the Presidency that could do that. Who negotiated with Kadijevic in the Presidency for the troops to come out of the barracks, I don't know, but it was never officially reported anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, that is the whole point. Even the president of the Presidency at the time, Jovic, was not aware of your intervention in Slovenia. So what you're now telling us at great length, quite unnecessarily, is absolutely untrue. And to prove that to you, I will quote from you this same stenographic report. It is on page 247 of that report. The last digits of the ERN number are 6140. And trying to respond to accusations against you by Kucan and others and myself to the effect that you had provoked the war in Slovenia, you even quote from your own decision, and you say yourself: "The Federal Executive Council took a decision on the implementation of federal regulations regarding the state border in Slovenia," et cetera. And then in the next paragraph, you say, and you quote from that decision: "Immediate enforcement of federal regulations will be achieved by the federal Ministry of the Interior in direct cooperation with the federal Secretariat for National Defence so as to engage border units of the JNA to secure the state border at border crossings and in inhabited areas in the border belt." So it was by your decision that you obliged your two federal ministries, the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of National Defence, to intervene in Slovenia. No one else knew about it, not even the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. You read out correctly this segment. The police of Yugoslavia was meant to get the cooperation of border units, those protecting the border and who do not have tanks or cannon but only light weapons, and to carry this out in cooperation with them. In the first place, that was not done. Neither the police nor the border units took part, but those that did take part were tanks and cannon and units that came out of the garrison. There were even units that came from Croatia. There were units from Istria, units from the surroundings of Zagreb. Therefore, someone had taken that decision. These were not border units but military units from several garrisons. We know that even some generals had problems afterwards because they had taken people along a 200-kilometre-long journey to reach Slovenia. No one else could have taken such a decision except the person who had the army under full control. And it was you, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, that had full control of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not right, Mr. Ante Markovic. You were the federal Prime Minister. You had the army under your control. And as for communication with the military leadership, in your schedule of responsibilities you can see how many times you met with the military or police leadership in the course of 1991 and how you acted as the most responsible person, as the president of the federal government of SFRY. And as regards what you said about my especially tense relationship --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have the occasion to answer, particularly important points which are made. The witness must have the answer -- chance to answer the allegations. Mr. Markovic, you've heard what the accused alleges. Perhaps you would care to respond, however briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I do not have all the documents that Mr. Milosevic has, and I am completely in an inferior position because I was unable to get anything from my office whereas he got everything. However, certain things are abundantly clear. If the government had been able to make decisions on how to use the army, then it would have been unnecessary to hold multiple sessions of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and take votes on using the army to calm the situation down in Yugoslavia. The Presidency discussed umpteen times, as well as at the closed sessions of the joint staff, this issue, and if the government had been able to decide on this, nobody would have bothered with the Presidency. So this is a blatant lie. We didn't stand a chance in all this affair. We had no communications with the army. If there had been communication between the government and the army and General Kadijevic who was in charge of the army and as such was accountable to the government, but in actual fact, he as a commander was completely subjected to the Presidency. The Federal Executive Council had nothing to do with it. I repeat, you can take original documents and read them. The only function according to which the army, or in this case General Kadijevic were a member of the army, were in terms of finance and administration. The federal government had no other competence over the army. And I would like to say once again, as far as Slovenia is concerned, units from garrisons with cannons, tanks, and other equipment were used, even units from the environs of Zagreb and from Croatia were used. And the phrasing in the decision of the federal government was that units that were already stationed on the border crossings should be used in cooperation with the police using only light weapons. But none of this was implemented. What was effected was an invasion. Who could have allowed this -- built this? In March 1990 when a huge number of people came out into the streets of Belgrade, over 100.000, to demonstrate against Mr. Milosevic, somebody decided to bring out tanks to stop them. Who was able to sanction this? Everything was done as it was done. Of course, formally Mr. Milosevic did not take this decision, but in actual fact he did. He was behind that, and he was behind what happened in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this so we can follow and make sure it's clear, and if you could keep the answers short, please. Did you have any control at all over the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you have direct -- any communication with the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I said, in administrative terms and financial terms, I did have contact with the army. Everything else was under the command of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you in a position to get the army to do anything or to ask them to do anything? Were they prepared to do it? Did you have any control over them at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. So help me God, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, what you're saying, is -- would that be confirmed by the constitutional system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely in accordance, in conformity with the constitutional system. Anyway, it's very logical. The army was financed from the budget of Yugoslavia. The budget of Yugoslavia was under the control of the Federal Executive Council. One item of this budget related to the army, and that was practically the only communication between the army and the federal government. There was no command or control communication, no information as to where units were deployed was given to the government, because that was not within our purview. Specialised functions of the army came under the exclusive competence of the Presidency, and the Presidency held many, many sessions to decide where and how the army would be used. All, all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Markovic, that is precisely the point. It is not in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dispute that under the constitution only the Presidency of Yugoslavia has the right to command the army, but in the instance of the war in Slovenia, which Kucan himself says was caused by the Federal Executive Council, it is obvious that you had abused and usurped the function of the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, bypassing the constitution, because you are quoting your own decision in this shorthand notes when you say that: "In the implementation of this decision, the Federal Executive Council will immediately cooperate, directly cooperate with the federal Ministry for National Defence in order to engage also the border units of the JNA." Therefore, with this decision of the government, you directly engage both the Ministry of National Defence and the Ministry of the Interior. And you are not engaging them in the financial sense as you are trying to represent. On the contrary. You are talking about using JNA units to carry out this decision of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fact that the constitution says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have the chance to answer these points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May. Would you kindly refrain from switching off my microphone before my sentence is over, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I shall cut off your microphone at any occasion when you abuse it, in particular by these over-lengthy questions which are not allowing witnesses to answer. The witness must have the opportunity to answer your question. You are simply to ask questions, not make speeches.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I will have to repeat what I have already said. Namely, in the conclusion it was written that the police, which had full competencies, should intervene on the Slovene border on behalf of the federal government and to reassert the governance of the federal government, because it was still one country. And when the police were doing their job on the border, they may also use certain border army units which are normally deployed there anyway. There was no mention of engaging army units on the border. So what was written about linking up with the border units was not actually -- did not actually happen, because the police never arrived on the border and had no chance to link up with border units. What happened was that the army came out of its border barracks and garrisons. Moreover, some units from Croatia were moved in with tanks and even air support. Somebody made a decision to do this. Who it was, I don't know. I didn't even know that this happened, because at 4.00 a.m. in the morning when all this took place, I was woken up by Milan Kucan who called me on the phone and told me, "Tanks are on the march through Slovenia." I said, "That's impossible. Why didn't you call the Presidency?" And Kucan says, "I cannot get through to them, and I can't speak to them, I can't find a common language with them anyway, but could you please try to put me through to the army." And then I helped him speak with Kadijevic. But I have to add one more thing. A couple of days later I boarded my plane with some of my associates, although everyone including Mesic, who was president of the Presidency, and the minister of foreign affairs of Croatia, who met me at the airport, were begging me not to go to Ljubljana, saying that I would be arrested there at the least and maybe even killed. However, I still went to Slovenia to stop this completely senseless war. And I think I succeeded in doing that. Moreover, when the army made the decision to bomb Ljubljana, I called up Kadijevic and told him, "You would then be bombing the Prime Minister as well, because I'm going to Ljubljana."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just do a couple of things. The exhibit that the accused was dealing with was indeed Exhibit 427, tab 6. We looked at it on the last occasion, and although I see that I didn't explain the problem to you, the problem is that it's only partially translated into English in that exhibit. The topics that the accused is raising now he actually raised on the last occasion after dealing with that exhibit, and indeed the questioning ended with Your Honour reminding him that we weren't directly concerned with Slovenia and invited him to turn to other topics, so that we parted from the exhibit at that stage. It remains only partially translated into English in 427, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We seem to have moved on from that. Thank you for that assistance to everybody. We'll move on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you mentioned heavy weaponry, tanks, artillery and so on and so forth. Where was it in Slovenia that the JNA used tanks and artillery? Where was tank or artillery fire used to destroy anything, to kill? Do you know of a specific instance of something like that happening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of more than one instance. There were many photographs of armoured unit upon armoured unit coming out into the streets of Slovenia. Armoured units accompanied by cannons, among other things, surrounded the airport of Ljubljana. They also landed in other cities. I, who was on my way to Ljubljana --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, could you please be more brief in answering. The airport of Ljubljana was a border crossing, and they did so following your decision. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't the case that they took over the border crossing, the only airport in Slovenia which is on the border, and blocked it. They were doing something else. That's what you're saying. Did somebody fire from these tanks?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These tanks were fired from, and there were dead, casualties. Not many, but there were. Moreover, when I arrived in Slovenia, I found out that a large number of tank units comprising young men had gone out completely unprepared, without supplies of water or food. They did not have the basic supplies of food or water, and they were completely left to their own devices, stranded. And it was I who organised that they get a shipment of food and water. And that time when I stayed for one day and one night, accompanied by other people because I wasn't alone, I tried to stop this war and save those people, and the result of my efforts was a success. It was a great success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this unfortunate war in Slovenia is your doing, and that is written in these decisions. And I'm now going to ask you a question relating to the alleged quarrel I had with Kucan. I never had any quarrel with Kucan. For instance, in these same shorthand notes, when Kucan is asking for the floor, page 243, ERN number ending with 521636, he says: "I am not going to be accountable to the Prime Minister," meaning you, "who now that he has lost the war," he is again speaking of you, "wants to achieve all this." That is in response to your advocacy of a certain programme. He says three proposals were made, complete with arguments, and he says that he agrees personally with the proposal and the economic plan presented by Slobodan Milosevic. So all this is happening after this unfortunate war where the president of Slovenia is addressing you, telling you what you had done in Slovenia. He's telling you that everyone in Slovenia knows that it was you who caused the war. And regarding various proposals made, he agrees with the one I made, not your proposal. How does that fit in with your story?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fits in very simply. Mr. Milosevic should answer this question: What had gone on before this? Is it true that Mr. Milosevic blocked the sale of Slovene goods in Serbia? Is it the case that Mr. Milosevic had severed economic links in Slovenia back in 1990? Is it also the case that Mr. Milosevic maintained other relations with Slovenia which considerably deteriorated other ties between Slovenia and Serbia involving Kosovo? When some units came from Slovenia to -- when Slovene people refused to go to Kosovo, how did Milosevic react to that? It all boils down to one thing. Mr. Milosevic maintained all the time relations with Slovenia that were very, very bad, and all his efforts were aimed at pushing Slovenia out of Yugoslavia for all practical purposes. How can Mr. Milosevic explain this? Why did Milosevic, Drnovsek, Jovic, and Kadijevic agree very easily that the army should pull out of Slovenia, although there was no official legal act to justify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, if possible let's try to speed things up, because Mr. Markovic [as interpreted] is not going to caution you by saying that you're making speeches. Since you're the one who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- some 200 and -- I forget now how many witnesses we're on now, 285, I think. You've allowed -- been allowed a great deal of time for cross-examination, so it is not fair for you to try and criticise witnesses in any way. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I think that the degree of protection that you afford witnesses is already a generally known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of this decision of yours that you quoted yourself and that I quoted to you only from these stenographic notes when you quoted it, how can you possibly say that as regards the events in Slovenia that took place on the basis of your decision were something that you heard about from Kucan and that you knew nothing about before that? You passed a decision. Your decision is being implemented, and you wonder over the implementation of this decision when the person upon whom this decision reflects calls you. Is there any logic in this, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. If it is correct what I said a few minutes ago, namely that the Federal Executive Council was not the one that passed this decision. Somebody else passed this decision, as was indeed was the case. Somebody else did pass this decision. The extent to which you personally were involved in this is something I cannot say, but your relationship with General Kadijevic is very well known. At that time he was already doing everything in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The real perpetrator is not here. The real perpetrator sits where you are sitting. And who then wanted to discredit the federal Prime Minister who was the only one who still had some kind of a reputation and who still had some support in the western world? This was a chance to discredit him. So that is Mr. Milosevic. That is what he did through Mr. Kadijevic. And that has nothing to do with the conclusions adopted by the Federal Executive Council. That directly pertained only to the borders that are protected by the police, and a border unit was supposed to assist them. In fact, what was carried out was an invasion of Slovenia with troops that were in garrisons, and the troops from the garrisons had come to Slovenia and started marching along Slovenian roads. They even put obstacles on their roads and there was even shooting there. Fortunately, not too many people were killed. As far as I can remember, there were 48 casualties altogether. But as far as I'm concerned, even if a single man loses his life, that is unforgivable. There is not a single objective that could justify or explain any such victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, most regrettably tens of soldiers were killed, as you had put it, quite innocent soldiers. They were killed in implementing your decision. And if you wanted to discredit yourself through your own decision, I don't know how you could link this decision up with somebody else's accountability except your own, you as president of the Federal Executive Council and head of the executive branch government at the time, at that time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat yet again that this has nothing to do with anything. If anybody reads the decision that was passed by the Federal Executive Council, they can see that it pertains to the police only and to border units that are very, very few in number. And who ordered tanks and cannons to appear? Who ordered the opening of garrisons? Who issued orders for the army to march from Croatia to Slovenia? Who? When Mr. Kucan called me, I had no idea whatsoever about this. After that, I had conversations about this within the government. I also talked about this to Veljko Kadijevic, and Veljko Kadijevic was then attacked at the government meeting too. He was told then that he acted outside any orders or approval. And who allowed him to do that? He answered to that that it was his duty to defend the borders of Yugoslavia and that no one had to instruct him to do that. And the question I would raise is why did he not do the same thing elsewhere? Why did he ask for the entire Presidency to give their consent? So someone had reached agreement with him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're the one.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heaven forbid. How could it be me? At the meeting of the Federal Executive Council, I had a public debate with him about this. So no way, it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you saw the consequences of your decision, of course you criticised the consequences of the decision that you took yourself. But let us establish some facts here, if possible, Mr. Markovic. Is it correct that on the 4th of July, 1991, a cease-fire was established and that, inter alia, a decision was reached to go back to the original state of affairs; to deblock the JNA units, the units and the institutions of the JNA, to return the resources of the JNA to the JNA, to re-establish communications, to set free prisoners? However, in spite of all of that, although the then-members of the Presidency from Macedonia and Bosnia, Tupurkovski and Bogicevic, were entrusted with carrying this out, do you recall that in spite of all of that the Slovenian leadership practically evaded the implementation of most of these things that I've quoted just now? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but I also remember that the Presidency of Yugoslavia and you, Mr. Milosevic, took part in that particular meeting too, and Drnovsek took part in it is well, that at that particular meeting a decision was reached to have all troops from Slovenia transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis -- on the basis of an agreement, including all the equipment they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to speed things up. We'll get to that too. But let us just look at something else. Do you remember something else? Do you remember that three days after that in Brioni a meeting was held? I did not attend that meeting in Brioni, but you did attend that meeting. So this was a meeting in the presence of the three ministers of the European Community at the time and a joint declaration was signed then. And it says there, inter alia, that the peoples of Yugoslavia are the only ones who can decide about their own future. So it's not the republics of Yugoslavia but the peoples of Yugoslavia that will decide on their own future. And what was agreed upon was that negotiations would take place. In this declaration, it said that unilateral steps should not be taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting that you're referring to, on the basis of the proposal of the Federal Executive Council that, by the way, I had drafted, a proposal was made to have a three-month moratorium. As a matter of fact, my first proposal was a six-month moratorium. However, it was believed then that this would not be accepted so we reduced it to three months. Through these three months we would actually carry out all the things that you are referring to just now, Mr. Milosevic. This three-month moratorium would make it possible for us to make the country capable of resolving its problems without resorting to war. As a matter of fact, this session that you've referred to just now, this session was held about a month after the Federal Executive Council had already prepared a proposal as to how the country would function during this moratorium period, and that was on the basis of what this discussion took place. And the borders were discussed in that context as well as this withdrawal. As a matter of fact, the core of this proposal went much deeper. It was supposed to go back to the status of the country that had existed before that, that people who had walked out of the Assembly should return to the Assembly, notably Slovenia and Croatia, in order to make it possible to reach decisions, any type of decisions that would be passed. If everybody is going to go their own ways, let the Assembly decide that, as was done later by the Assembly of Czechoslovakia. So let us part our ways without a conflict. Let's create pre-conditions, after all, for somehow bringing yet another kind of Yugoslavia together that would hinge on a minimum. However, this was made totally impossible to have these three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Markovic. Your answer is yes, I assume, in response to my question, because I said that in the presence of the European troika, this declaration was made, and what I quoted is written in this declaration. I assume that your answer is yes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave an expanded answer in terms of the total question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Markovic. Is it correct that the leadership of Slovenia did not fulfil their obligations from this declaration?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct irrespective of the fact that you said before that that you agreed with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not agree with them at all.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aha. You did not agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I personally never had any quarrels with Kucan. That is a completely different matter. I did not agree with their policy, of course, because I did not agree with secession.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't want it to seem now that it is only the Slovenians who are to be blamed for that. Everybody is. You too. You also asked for the moratorium to be carried out in the following way: If not voluntarily, we are going to do what we want to do by force. On several occasions that was pointed out during that session, and I intervened and said, "These countries are --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me which session?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same one you mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, find it. Where is it written here?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably I don't have it. You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said somebody should do something by force or would do something by force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Jovic said that several times, and I intervened and I said, "Do you think that through force and punishment you're going to resolve this?" And he said, "What's going to happen if you don't -- if they don't pay customs duty again?" Then Jovic said, "You keep on negotiating all the time." And I said, "But you are -- you are talking about force too."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my questions, Mr. Markovic. You answered one of them, and you regretted that, and now you don't really want to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a fair comment as far as the witness is concerned. Ask him proper questions and you can do it, but trying to make scores off the witness, they don't assist you or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm just trying to have the truth revealed here. Fortunately, truth -- the truth is a very powerful thing, and it will always prevail, here too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Markovic, that during the conflicts in Slovenia 44 members of the JNA lost their lives, namely six officers, six NCOs, 30 soldiers and cadets and one civilian employed in the army and one unidentified person? And also, there were 184 wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the gravest crimes committed against the JNA soldiers were when the paramilitary formations were then established in Slovenia, when they brought children of officers who were underaged to five border posts and threatened to kill them unless their fathers surrendered? And also, they subjected them to other kinds of pressures, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. psycho-physical torture. That's what happened vis-a-vis the members of the JNA. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the first thing. I do not remember the second thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first thing, yes. The killings, you mean, the woundings. And tell me then, at that time you were Prime Minister. What did you do in order to have the perpetrators of these crimes brought to justice? Did you make any effort aimed at that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again I will have to repeat that while no one, including Mr. Milosevic, made any effort whatsoever in order to stop this war --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took a plane --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You already talked about that, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer. You're asking me whether I did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you did anything. I am asking you in relation to the crimes committed. Did you do anything as federal Prime Minister in order to have the perpetrators brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again I have to repeat that I intervened in order to bring the war to an end and not to have further loss of lives. I have to say objectively now that my trip to Slovenia then bordered on death, but I did that. Secondly, if people were supposed to be punished then, there were appropriate judicial authorities to carry that out. There are military authorities. There are civilian authorities, depending on who was under which jurisdiction. I do not remember that any government in any part of the world would try anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall any such thing either, but usually all of this is being placed under some kind of responsibility of mine, although I was not the judiciary or the legislation, and I did not command the army either. So did you take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask -- you can certainly ask the witness if he took any action, but my recollection is that Mr. Kucan was asked about these matters and gave evidence about them, who was able to do so. Perhaps the witness can say if he's got anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you remember that when we were talking about Slovenia, Slovenia in 1989, 1990 and 1991 adopted a whole series of laws unilaterally actually undermining the legal order of Yugoslavia? For instance, the amendments to the constitution of Slovenia in 1989, then the constitutional law to implement the amendments in the area of national defence, then the law to stop all proceedings that had been started if they come under the federal laws. In other words, they annulled all federal laws. Then there was the declaration on sovereignty of Slovenia, then the plebiscite on independence and autonomy of Slovenia, then a whole series of other documents. I don't wish to quote all of them because they would take too much time. A whole page could be written listing all those documents of which you are well aware. Did the constitutional law review them all and establish that they were unconstitutional and they had them annulled? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, but I would like to tell you the context within which I remember them. In the first place, it was not Slovenia in 1989 or in 1990 that it undertook those steps but later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Weren't the amendments to the constitution adopted in 1989? Were they or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer fairly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The elections in Slovenia were carried out sometime between the spring and the summer of 1990. So this happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not talking about the elections but the amendments to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you remember when Serbia blocked Slovenian goods? When did it block economic relations with Slovenia? When did Serbia, or, rather, you personally made a breakthrough into the monetary fund, into the budget and took, or not to say steal 18.2 billion dinars, which is two and a half billion German marks? Don't you think that all this affected the other republics?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the relationships between the central banks of the republics and the central bank of Yugoslavia can be found in documents. There can be no theft. Whether you go beyond a certain limit or not, this becomes immediately visible. You will admit that all this is highly transparent. It is not possible in -- to do anything affecting monetary flow secretly. And then those relationships are later corrected, adjusted, balanced out, et cetera. You were an economist; surely you know that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I do. But I also know quite clearly that you took a decision to take 18.2 billion from the central bank to the Bank of Serbia for which you had absolutely no right to do. You had no right. And by doing that, you actually carried out a diversion, an act of sabotage against the whole Yugoslav system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, let us not go into monetary issues. If somebody makes a primary issue for the purchase of wheat, that is not a blow against the monetary system. This is something that can later be regulated through mutual relations between the central banks and the banks of the republics, and this is something that happened frequently. It has nothing do with your exaggerations describing it as Serbia's incursion, as Serbia's theft, or anything like that. So let's not use such descriptions.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that 18.2 billion dinars is a small sum, and this is a sum that was established -- tell me, was it established or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of the figure that was involved, but I do know that someone was repeatedly -- various republics in various conditions went beyond their limits. Later on this was ironed out in mutual relationships, but that can easily be established, because all those monetary flows are transparent. Primary issue is evident, and this can be traced in the documents of the central bank and nothing can be concealed.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one until then nor since then, I would be bold to say, carried out such a theft of money that it was not entitled to as the Republic of Serbia had done, or, rather, Mr. Milosevic. The more so as even what you say, that it could have been used for agriculture, that its primary issue could be used for agriculture, in those days issues of the National Bank of Yugoslavia could not be used for agriculture or anything else. We financed those needs through the budget. And thirdly, any decision regarding primary issue had to be made by the council of the National Bank of Yugoslavia. And it was the only body competent for such decisions. Now, if you know that, when did this council meet to allow 18.2 billion to be transferred to your account?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course those decisions of the council of governors cannot -- without such a decision of the council of governors, no one could do any such thing. That is not in dispute. And it is also not in dispute that what you are talking about was not known in public. Why are you using such ugly words like "theft"? Why are you demeaning yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for considering my position, but that was not true. And it wasn't known until I revealed it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we first spoke, you said you had no idea.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said then was quite true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to in particular refer to the accused, that you must allow a chance for somebody to interpret. Our interpreters have a lot of hard work, they keep up very well, but they should be given a chance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will try to speak more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, but time is flying and Mr. Markovic is explaining at great length some matters which I'm not even asking him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it in dispute that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia annulled the decision taken by Slovenia? Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of those, yes. They annulled them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that during your term in office Slovenia ignored the institutions, law and constitution of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it didn't but later on it did. But also I wish to mention here that the Federal Executive Council had proposed an amendment to the constitution which would establish different relations and elections throughout Yugoslavia, but the fact is that Serbia and Slovenia from two different points of view prevented this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not true, but we'll come to that too. You say that the decision on the withdrawal of the army was taken by the Presidency. When I say the withdrawal of the army, I mean from Slovenia, that it was taken by the Presidency under Milosevic's influence. That is what you said. Now, my question is: Who voted in favour of pulling out the Yugoslav People's Army from Slovenia? Do you remember that this was a decision taken by the Presidency? So the presidents of the republics don't have a vote. That the Presidency, all of the members except Mesic voted in favour of the army being pulled out of Slovenia. Mesic voted against the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The -- let the witness must have a chance. You've been talking for at least a minute. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. A meeting of the Presidency consisted of several parts, I would say. First there was some discussion as to how to strengthen the position of the army in Slovenia, and then as far as I remember, the proposal came from Mr. Jovic that the possibility of withdrawing the army also be discussed. And this was immediately accepted by the army, and they immediately elaborated on the idea. So clearly such an agreement had already been reached by certain officials as a final solution, for otherwise Kadijevic would not have so readily accepted it. And then it -- an agreement was easily reached to pull out the army. At that meeting, it is true, as Milosevic says, that everyone voted except Mesic. I think that Tupurkovski didn't vote either, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tupurkovski and Bogicevic agreed, being convinced that that would avoid a conflict.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't agree with it but I had no right to vote. My vote didn't count at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I did not attend, and I -- as I am not a member of the Presidency, and I'm speaking on the basis of documents. Therefore all the members with the exception of Mesic voted in favour of pulling out the army from Slovenia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: As far as I know, Tupurkovski voted against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That can be easily established. Even if Tupurkovski had voted against, which he didn't, because he felt that was a way of avoiding the conflict, the vote would still be 6 to 2. Therefore, is it clear that your statement that the decision on the withdrawal of Slovenia -- of the army from Slovenia was taken under Milosevic's influence is completely unfounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept that, because certain things that are done behind the scenes, and that was the case here, everything had been prepared before people came to the session, things are not resolved at meetings. Things had been prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So I had influence over all the members of the Presidency, over a sufficient number except Mesic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even remember whether Bogicevic attended the meeting, but I think Tupurkovski also voted against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. The things you don't remember, I won't ask you about. Is it true that the JNA left Slovenia without armaments, without its weaponry, that everything it had it left behind in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely untrue that it took everything?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. The army couldn't take everything. What it couldn't take, it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is also untrue what you said in paragraph 13 of your statement, that the JNA withdrew from Slovenia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The JNA withdrew from Slovenia to all the other Yugoslav republics with the exception of Croatia, because the leadership of Croatia at the time was opposed to a part of the army staying in the territory of Croatia. So then the troops from Slovenia went to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to Serbia and to Macedonia and to Montenegro. Therefore, in a dispersed manner, it went to all the other republics. Is that right, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not right. Some smaller units did go to Serbia or Montenegro. As far as I recall, none went to Macedonia. On the contrary, the withdrawal of the army from Macedonia was under preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you're right. Not to Macedonia but to all the other republics.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish? So no one went to Macedonia. Now, whether troops went to Serbia, I believe they did, some to Montenegro perhaps as well, but most of the bulk of the troops went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there is plenty of evidence to be found of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is one of principle. The army that withdrew from Slovenia withdrew to other parts of the territory of the SFRY where the JNA was at the time the only legal armed force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but at the same time it was legal throughout, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was the legal force. Why didn't it all go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why should it all go to Serbia? Serbia and the SFRY was not one and the same.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would Bosnia-Herzegovina and the SFRY be one and the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it did go to Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some smaller units that were unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can easily establish which units went where. We don't have to do that today. But the point is that the army withdrew to other parts of SFRY. As for the army in Croatia, the part from Slovenia didn't go to Croatia, but there was JNA -- there were JNA troops in Croatia there, and they were legal.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there and they were legal. But those troops from Slovenia didn't go to Croatia. That is a fact. And it is also a fact that smaller units went to Serbia and Montenegro. And it is also a fact that the bulk of those forces went to Bosnia, because it was known that a war was in the offing in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you knew that because you were the federal Prime Minister and Bosnia-Herzegovina was under your competence, but for the -- to say that the army went to Bosnia to prepare war, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You knew that better than me because you organised part of that war in agreement with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. I can't wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is also untrue what you say in paragraph 24 of your statement. Boro Jovic was never consulted in connection with the JNA intervention in Slovenia, nor was that ever discussed with you. He was never consulted about that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was consulted, nor did I discuss that with him. I just said that two of us had discussed that later and that he held one position, I another. If you read that carefully, you would see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Markovic. Is it in dispute that you had not only de jure responsibility throughout that period, 1989, 1990, and 1991, because you were throughout the federal Prime Minister, but in addition to that de jure responsibility, you also had a number of meetings and engaged in various activities in the federal government with all the important departments of government throughout that period and de facto performed those duties in 1989, 1990, and 1991? Last time I provided that schedule for 1991, and similar ones could be found for 1989 and 1990. So both de jure and de facto you were the executive power at the head of the pyramid of executive powers in SFRY. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would ask you kindly - and I apologise to the Court for saying this - if I could have a copy of those documents which actually belong to me and you have them. Maybe I will need them when I decide to write my memoirs. I was unable to get hold of those documents. It is a fact that my government -- I say "mine" of course in quotation marks. I could say the Federal Executive Council, of which I was the president, functioned well in the course of 1989 and 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw what happened in 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already at the end of 1990 certain things happened which seriously jeopardised the already limited competencies that the federal government had. Nowhere in Europe can you find a government with such modest and limited competencies as was the case with the Yugoslav government, whereas you, with your incursion into the payment system and the monetary system, when you took 18.2 billion dinars, by doing this, the little authority the government had, which relied on personalities rather than actual rights, you called even those limited powers into jeopardy. Regardless of the fact that I held that position and despite the fact that I communicated a lot with other people, the truth is that my ability, my capacities were reduced from one day to the next. I devoted most of my efforts to preventing war and the dissolution of Yugoslavia. To that end, I toured all the republics. I spoke to them. I went to the Assembly of Slovenia. I held a speech there that is well known, which was meant to convince the Assembly to change its decision. I went to the Assembly of Croatia, and I spoke there for the first time in a way I never spoke before, and I said some major things there. Let me not repeat those things. If necessary, I can do that. I also asked to be given the possibility to speak in the Republic of Serbia. I was given that approval in principle, but I was not given a chance of speaking in the Republic of Serbia. Though when I look back at those events those were Don Quixotic events of mine, to save something that couldn't be saved, but as an individual I even resorted to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come for a break. We will try and ensure that the witness has the document which he has asked to see. He should be entitled to see that. We think we may have it, but we will, during the adjournment, the half an hour break, we will see that he gets it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I remember that several days ago Mr. Nice asked you for permission to give the witness this 1991 schedule as the witness asked him for that, and you gave him that permission. Now, why that didn't happen is perhaps an omission on Mr. Nice's part, or maybe an omission on the part of the witness to pick up the document, but I remember very well that this request was made of you and that you granted it, because it was a document reviewing his obligations and activities in 1991, and he obviously has that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll look at that. We're now going to adjourn. We will take the usual break, 20 minutes. We've found, I think, I will be grateful to the registry, the figure seems to be Defence Exhibit 207, and the witness should have a copy that he can review during the break. Yes, we will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Markovic did not receive the document that he sought and for which permission was obtained to provide him. I don't know why that is. We certainly sent it. I'll find out what the problem was. I'm sorry. I apologise to Mr. Markovic that he didn't receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I hope Mr. Markovic will receive it sooner or later, at least, for his memoirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the point I wanted to raise is this: It is not in dispute, Mr. Markovic that at the time of the aggravation of the Yugoslav crisis in 1989 when Slovenia adopted its amendments and in 1990 and 1991, and on top of that there was arming at the time, the creation of first paramilitary formations and various conflicts. It is not in dispute that you had a full overview of the events and the instruments available to you in the form of state instruments.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in dispute that the Federal Executive Council has an arsenal of these powers, but this was a very modest arsenal, and in every area related to the army, directly or indirectly, the so-called defence, the federal government had no competencies whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since my time is extremely limited, I will provide you with an overview of your activities for 1989 similar to the one for 1991 as well as for year 1990. And if you compare 1989 and 1990 and 1991, you can see that the method of work is the same, and the method of communication with all the important factors that were subjected to the federal government were the same in relation to both the police and the army and all the other agencies. I am not able now to go through all of these activities of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I want to tender them, Mr. May. And since these are originals, I would like copies returned to me, including the copy for 1991 that I already provided. And I absolutely don't mind that Mr. Markovic should receive a copy of this overview, because it will certainly be useful to him when he writes his memoirs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now in return, I would appreciate brief answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. If you want to put the papers in now, we will consider the position, and we will consider them to -- just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1990 and 1989. The one for 1990 I already -- the one for 1991 I provided already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What I shall do is -- Mr. Nice, if you would look at those documents. They are not in English, but perhaps at least the Prosecution can give us a view as to if there is any objection to admitting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From this we can see that in 1989, in 1990, and 1991 you had regular meetings with the army, the police, the Presidency, with your own members of the government, with officials of various republics, with republican delegations, including those of Slovenia, Serbia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and so on and so forth. So it is indisputable that over those three years you held executive power in Yugoslavia at the time when these events took place. I don't think you will challenge that, will you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for showing that I have been quite active in this period. This extensive activity of mine in this period does not mean that I had actual power in whatever I was doing. You characterised my own work as being of negotiating character. Using my own methods, I was looking for a solution, trying to avoid Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflict and dissolution of Yugoslavia, and to that end I engaged all the forces that were available to me. I toured, tested, looked for people who were willing to help me to prevent a war, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, you say with regard to the army that you only had competencies in the administrative and financial sense, but I will now show you a document that I received from the side opposite, which is an excerpt from some sort of shorthand notes that I was not provided with in its entirety. The ERN number is 01024563, and from this we can see that General Kadijevic informs you, for instance, of the casualties in Slovenia, of inter-ethnic conflicts, arming activities, et cetera. And then he says, "Losses in Slovenia, 44 killed, 144 wounded." Ante Markovic says, "First you said it was 298 in total." Kadijevic says, "In inter-ethnic conflicts and other conflicts in Yugoslavia, the total was 298 only for this year." Markovic says, "How many were wounded?" Kadijevic answers, "472, and the total is 770, and there are other conflicts." He mentions Kosovo, the north of Macedonia, Sandzak. And from this it is clear that you are discussing the security situation with the minister of defence. And we can also see in these agendas of yours various meetings to discuss the security situation, the activities of the army and the police, not only financing aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please. If I may assist the Court. This document was tendered through Mr. Mesic. It's 328, Exhibit 328, tab 16. What is now being shown to the witness is contained in this document. So we can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we've interrupted the flow, there is no reason to object to these documents on the grounds that they may not be what the accused says they are. They're similar in category to the document that should have been provided in copy to the witness over the adjournment, and the Chamber will recall my observations on the last occasion about how surprised I was that the accused had access to this original material when it hadn't been available to us or to the witness, but there is no reason to doubt they are what they are. Whether they merit becoming an exhibit is a matter for the Chamber. They're quite voluminous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in due course when we've had a moment we will allow the witness to see those documents, but let us not for the moment interrupt the flow of the examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just quoted to you from the document I received from the side opposite. I believe it is authentic. We can see that General Kadijevic is reporting to you on all these events, that you are discussing them with him. So there is no question that you are discussing the financing of the army or anything else which would be in the exclusive competence of the federal government. You are discussing military activities. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have this document. So as far as this document is concerned, I cannot give any opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I can be of assistance again. This is another exhibit that has been introduced, and it is available in the language Mr. Markovic understands, in B/C/S. I can give him a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that I don't need this document now because I have no time to study it here. Mr. Milosevic obviously studied it already. I can answer without looking at the document. It is logical for a president of an institution, including the president of a government, to discuss with his Ministers something that falls under their purview. I did have such discussions with all Ministers. And if Mr. Milosevic is consistent, he will admit that I had such discussions with other Ministers much more often than I talked to Mr. Kadijevic about his sphere of work. Another thing, within the Presidency of Yugoslavia, there is a sector that is in charge of security issues, and that sector comprises representatives of various institutions, including representatives of the federal government, and briefings are held there too in that sector for the purpose of preparing Federal Cabinet meetings to discuss such issues. It is also logical for the Prime Minister to be interested in the progress of the harvest, the situation in tourism, the situation concerning commodity reserves, monetary issues, financial situation, the problems of banks, and various other issues including those that relate to the army. I don't see how a high official is supposed to lead his agency without being informed of its work. But that is one thing. It is quite another thing to have direct control and command over something. When the army is concerned, things are defined very clearly in the constitution. I suggest we don't waste much more time over this. The army is within the competence of the Presidency of Yugoslavia under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. I'm just saying that you are discussing with the Minister of Defence military activities, not those things which you claim are your exclusive competence.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that does not mean that I am taking military decisions. I am only being briefed on what is going on, and that is very logical. I am being briefed as the Prime Minister. But as far as decision-making is concerned, heaven forbid. It was just an insinuation the way you tried to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said what I said about your role in the war in Slovenia, and I need not go back to it. But here is another thing relating to Dubrovnik, a report by Hrvoje Kacic of the 1st of October, 1991, ERN numbers ending with 75129. We all attended that conference in The Hague; you, I, representatives of all republics, members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. All of us were there. And they say here there are problems around Dubrovnik, and they say if you can't talk to Jokic, who came to replace Djurovic, who was killed and who used to be the commander, here in The Hague they have Kadijevic and the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Ante Markovic. So concerning this event in Dubrovnik, even those people who were in charge of Croatia put you in the foreground. They say you have Kadijevic here in The Hague and Prime Minister Ante Markovic, and they rely on you to deal with these problems. And then reference is made to the officials of Montenegro, because this is in the immediate vicinity of Montenegro. And there is no reference to Serbia. How can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have this document either, and I don't know what it says, so I cannot check whether -- what it really says is what you quote or maybe it is something different, but it is a fact that the war that was waged there in Dubrovnik but also in Vukovar, if you wish, and in other parts of Croatia, this war was something that the Prime Minister, the federal Prime Minister Ante Markovic had nothing to do with. Ante Markovic took every possible measure to prevent this war. And in this context, precisely at that session Mr. Milosevic referred to, I asked him, "Can you see what's going on in Vukovar? Can you see that Dubrovnik is being shelled?" He said, "Are you mad? Who would be crazy enough to bomb Dubrovnik?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
