utterances.text: Who said that? Yes, that's what I said. It was madness.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I replied, "Let's go and see Tudjman." And I said to Tudjman, who was there with his escorts Saronjic and other people, I said to Tudjman, "I'm speaking to Milosevic about the bombing, the shelling of Dubrovnik, and he's telling me that Dubrovnik is not being shelled. He's telling me it's not true." And I wrote in the end what Tudjman's answer was: "Milosevic says it is not being shelled, otherwise, I would have known about it." And the fact is that Dubrovnik was shelled. There are photographs about that. There is even a brief film about it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say at any point I would have known if it was shelled. I said, "Who would be mad enough to do that?"

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a film about that. You said, "Who would be mad enough to do that," but you also said, "If it were true, I would know about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I only quoted to you one sentence from this report of Hrvoje Kacic, the ERN number ending with 7529. Those who have it in front of them can compare. The sentence reads, "If you cannot talk with Jokic who came to replace Djurovic who was killed, you have here in The Hague Kadijevic and Prime Minister Markovic."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which way was Hrvoje Kacic competent? You could have named anybody. Tell me who this Kacic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he was a Croatian official at the time, who is relying upon you to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have done better to rely on you. He would have had a better chance of resolving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am quoting him, and you know better than I do who Kacic is. Now, look what it says further on. As Spegelj says, and I suppose you know who he is, you were playing two cards. Here is what Spegelj said to Vladimir Jagar. You not only provided Spegelj with data and information saying that you don't like Serbia and you would not leave Serbia until you managed to take over - that is ERN number 01112475 - it says: "Spegelj told me he has a man in Belgrade who says he can effect an arrest of him. He says army has the intention of arresting him. Spegelj says he got this information from Ante Markovic who advised him on the same occasion that he should leave Belgrade, otherwise the army would arrest him." So instead of preventing this illegal transport of arms that Spegelj was involved in, you call Spegelj on the phone and warn him that he should run away before being arrested by the army for this illegal arms delivery.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me when this was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope I can. It's the minutes from the 18th February 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were times when telephone communication between Serbia and Croatia, Belgrade and Zagreb did not exist at all. Very often I had to phone through Sarajevo or through some other institution. Another thing, I did not see or talk to Spegelj at that time at all, and I had nothing to do with Mr. Spegelj at the time. I had no need to have any communication with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll quote to you very shortly again from page 01112478, where it says: "At this meeting somebody asked Spegelj, what's the situation with Ante Markovic? And in this connection, Spegelj said, Ante Markovic, Prime Minister, is a person playing two cards. He's very fond of power. He said that he, Markovic, cannot stand Milosevic or Serbia, and until he destroys Milosevic and Serbia, he will not leave Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I have to do with the private opinions of Spegelj? Anybody, Tom, Dick, or Harry could say here you have Milosevic and here you have Markovic; Markovic hates Milosevic. This has no importance at all. He is not someone who is close to me. I didn't socialise with him. I had nothing to do with Spegelj so he cannot know what I thought. He used this for some purpose of his own. This has nothing to do with me. And anyway, I believe there are many other arguments, many other materials that could clearly prove who advocated what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that what Spegelj says and what pertains to your assessment in terms of your behaviour and attitude toward Serbia, that that is all simply incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you something else. Since it is being claimed here that some kind of a plan for a Greater Serbia existed, and you say that too, in the opinion of this other side it -- this was controlled. So now I'm going to show you what you said at the session of the Presidency in July 1991. This is a long document, stenographic notes. I was not present at the session, but I am going to quote to you something from page 61. The ERN number is 02017995. Ante Markovic says --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we do all that, the accused knows quite well we can't just pull out ERN numbered documents, probably provided under substantial Rule 68 disclosure, like that, and of course the documents come with no observation as to their truth value. It would help the witness probably, he doesn't seem to have any trouble with the documents so far but it would probably help if he could at least see the document and follow it. We can't produce it just on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, of course not. But so far we have in fact not done too badly considering the difficulties which we're in, given an accused in person, one who is liable to quote very large parts of -- voluminously from documents. At the same time, he is in person and we have to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll do our best to check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will ask him to quote it. We will ask you to pursue it if you would. Yes, what is this document you want to quote to the witness again, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is called Stenographic Notes from the 125th session of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, held on the 12th of July of 1991, starting at 10.30 a.m., and it also says that it's strictly prohibited to have this document copied. It is a strictly confidential document. Of course Mr. Nice has this. I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where was this session held?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume in Belgrade. It doesn't say where it was held, but it does say, "After using this document, return it to the general secretary of the Presidency of the SFRY, Presidency of the SFRY, Stjepan Mesic," et cetera. Now I'm quoting Stjepan Mesic, who is chairing the meeting, and he says, "I give the floor to Ante," and then a brief quotation. "We noted that actually things are progressing autonomously, in a spontaneous manner, that they are getting out of control increasingly and that this getting out of control applies to all segments, actually, not only in terms of mutual conflicts. And on this basis, certain units are being established. They have started to operate autonomously, but this also pertains to the economic and social fields. There is deep erosion," and so on and so forth. So you yourself say that things are progressing in a spontaneous manner and that they cannot be controlled. They're getting out of control. And then on the next page you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we can't possibly deal with this in that way. It's very hard at all for the witness to be able to deal with it, and I'm going to ask him if he can remember - he's remembered, remarkably, several things - whether he can remember this and whether he can answer in order to try and save time and get on. But we have a note from the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I believe - I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich - this is 328, tab 16. It was something produced for identification and therefore is in B/C/S but is not translated. It's a voluminous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask the witness about it first of all. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember this, but it's a bit some -- it's a bit different from what Mr. Milosevic just said. This is an assessment of part of the process that was evolving at that time and that was initiated from other quarters. It is also true that in the materials I did write, I mean the ones that I worked on and that I wrote for the OTP, Mr. Milosevic never advocated a Greater Serbia in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I also wrote that in fact he worked in favour of one, but he never advocated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You stated here that things are developing spontaneously, and then you're saying the situation is getting out of control and the governments and republics and even individuals, highly authoritative individuals, can no longer control various events and so on and so forth. So you're talking about a general erosion. Is that right, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to know which time period this refers to, where this can be incorporated, because you see, when you extract a quotation like this, it can be just out there hanging in the air. It can be about anything. Since I do not know all the things that were being discussed there and in connection with what, I would not be in a position to give an accurate answer. If I could have the opportunity of studying this, I could certainly be in a position to give an answer. I do remember that this was discussed, but it was discussed in the context of overall developments in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Markovic, as far as the time period is concerned, this is a session of the 12th of July, 1991. I am not going to burden you with quotations from this session any longer. This also has to do with your quotation, but I don't want you to make any comments but -- in any other way except for what you actually said. A few minutes ago, I also quoted you, only I did not draw any conclusions. You say: "In our assessment, there is a central issue which is one of the basic issues in our country." That is what you say. And that is the relationship between the Serbs and Croats or, rather, between Serbia and Croatia. So is your position clear, therefore? I also believed, and I still believe today, that this was the key relationship, that this was the central issue, as you had put it, one the basic issues in our country, that is the relationship between the Serbs and Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer now? Several times I presented that point of view. I would take up a lot of time now, so I can't go into all of this, and I cannot explain what the first meeting between Tudjman and myself was like. We had not known each other before. We met one evening in Zagreb, in the offices that I had in Zagreb as federal Prime Minister, and we talked for over two hours. There were five conclusions. One of these five conclusions was Serbs should be talked to within Croatia, not via Serbia itself and Milosevic. Secondly, when I spoke in the Croatian parliament, I think it was towards the end of May or beginning of June, but at any rate before any decisions were made. I said then, because I went there to intervene, in order to prevent the decisions that were being prepared then for the parliament of Croatia. I made a long speech there, and I said that among other things. And also, as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned too. So Serbs should be talked to in Croatia, not via Serbia and via Milosevic. I thought that was a sine qua non.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sine qua non. That is what I claimed too, that that was the key issue, the relationship between the Serbs and Croats, and that is what you say, or, rather, the relationship between Serbia and Croatia. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. After that, you reached a very nice agreement. You did with Tudjman in Karadjordjevo. Milosevic and Tudjman agreeing in Karadjordjevo that they would split up Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true but we're going to get to that as well. I just wanted to clarify this particular matter, that the key issue in our country is the relationship between Serbs and Croats or, rather, the relationship between Serbia and Croatia, because here this is being presented in a distorted fashion. I am glad that you explained it in the same way. Mr. Markovic, you said that I wanted to put everything under the control of the army, and I had control over the army, and I had control over the members of the Presidency. In this very same document, the stenographic minutes, this is what one of the members of the Presidency says. This is the member of the Presidency from Vojvodina, Jugoslav Kostic. Jugoslav Kostic says: "I am not prepared to vote for that solution which would give the army carte blanche to secure the state border by force," and so on. So isn't it clear that Serbia and what you called the Serbian bloc was not in favour of giving the army a free hand so that it could secure the state border? And then he adds: "When we see that there are flags of the Republic of Slovenia on the state border and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's quite impossible for a witness to deal with this length. Now, we've allowed some leeway because of the need for time, but we must also be fair to the witness in order that he could answer what's being put. Mr. Markovic, I don't know if you could briefly deal with what is being alleged at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very interesting that Milosevic extracted only a very partial element that speaks of relations between the army and Serbia and relations within the Presidency of Yugoslavia. It is well known, and I believe there is no need to prove this, that in the Presidency of Yugoslavia as the Supreme Commander that the army was subordinated to there were two groups within the Presidency. In one group was Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia. And the other group consisted of Serbia, Vojvodina, Kosovo, and Montenegro. That is four to four. So why were these sessions held so many times in order to get a majority? If that had been Kostic's vote, then it would have been rejected. But the fact remains that sessions were held, even sometimes in army premises where it was very cold. And they sought to break Bogicevic's will and to make him vote in favour of giving the army a free hand in order to deal with the situation in Yugoslavia. However, they did not succeed in that. Bogicevic, although he was a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was accused of being a traitor. So this one example that Mr. Milosevic quoted doesn't really mean much. As the Germans say, one swallow does not bring spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs say the same thing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm German oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this shows no doubt that there was no agreement involved within this Serbian Bloc, as you call it, because Kostic is opposing this proposal to give the army a free hand to secure the state borders. I'm not going to keep you any long with these stenographic notes, but please, since my time is restricted, give me answers that are as brief as possible. Is it correct that at that time at the peak of your term of office only Croatia and Slovenia opposed the quest for a constitutional setup of Yugoslavia that would be reformed on the basis of the existing constitution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Federal Executive Council also asked for a constitutional change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what I'm saying, that only Slovenia and Croatia were opposed to finding a constitutional solution for a future Yugoslavia on the basis of the existing constitution?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not exactly the way it was. On the 18th of December, 1989, when I presented my programme of reform, then the Federal Executive Council presented as a prerequisite for carrying out this reform, and also for continuing the reforms that were already taking place, requested that the constitution of Yugoslavia be changed then, and this change of the constitution was supposed to make it possible to carry out elections throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, this was prevented by the delegates from Slovenia and the delegates from Serbia. The delegates from Croatia were prepared to support this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. That is not correct. The delegates from Serbia tried to prevent this. Do you remember that the Presidency of Yugoslavia -- I'm not talking about the Federal Executive Council now, your Federal Executive Council. But the Presidency of Yugoslavia in mid-1989 launched an initiative to change the constitution of the SFRY. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a change of the constitution of the SFRY had started already in 1996 [as interpreted] when these governments were not even in place. After all, I was a member of this constitutional changes commission. We had been working on that for two years, so some changes had already been effected. Other changes that were being sought, well that is true, the Presidency did ask for them.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also then in 1989, the Federal Executive Council sought changes but the way they saw them, not the way the Presidency of Yugoslavia saw them. And as for these changes that were sought by the Federal Executive Council, a vast majority were in favour of most of them. However, as regards multi-party elections throughout Yugoslavia, all Yugoslav elections, the representatives of Slovenia and Serbia were not in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. The representatives of Serbia were in favour of multi-party elections. And do you remember that on the 28th of May, 1990, in the federal executive -- in the Federal Assembly, the representative of Serbia asked for the right to secession to be regulated by law in order to prevent any kind of tensions or to avoid chaos, to have all of this regulated by law?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time the Federal Assembly, meeting on the 29th of May, 1990, supported the right to self-determination, including the right to secession?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was only then that the law was adopted enabling elections at the level of the whole of Yugoslavia, only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what was the main idea behind that proposal; to ensure protection of fundamental human rights, a peaceful settlement of disputes, equality of all the Yugoslav peoples, and all this was built into this proposal of the Presidency, as you know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was so, but very often what was written in documents wasn't so important. What was important was the way they were implemented, and they weren't implemented very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember after extensive procedure in preparing the amendments four republics and two provinces submitted a proposal on the constitutional reconstruction of Yugoslavia to the Federal Assembly, and four republics plus two provinces submitted a unified proposal on the constitutional reconstruction of Yugoslavia, while simultaneously Slovenia and Croatia submitted a proposal on confederation? An agreement was not reached as there was no consensus. But it wasn't Serbia that had a different concept than Slovenia and Croatia, but the ratio was 6 to 2. Is that right, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the discussion you are referring to took place mostly at meetings of the presidents of the Presidencies of the republics and provinces. And you moved from one town to the next, discussing these matters. You excluded the rest of us from these discussions because you were the actual people in power. That is, the republics rather than the federal institutions. None of us attended those talks, and that is where you differed. Among other things, at one of those meetings, I think it was the representative of Croatia or Slovenia, I don't remember exactly who, when he proposed that a confederation be opted for, you used the well-known expression "Malo Morgen." This could also be an indication who you're close to. So you see, you showed an inclination that you accused me of a moment ago, an inclination towards Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't speak German, but in Serbia very often the expression is used, "Malo Morgen," meaning never, really.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously there were two ideas, a loose confederation was one option, and the other one. And you were in favour of the other option. You headed that option and would not accept any kind of compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was a precise one. I am not talking about meetings of the presidents of the republics, because when you say "you," you mean presidents of the republics; not just me but all the presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You excluded the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I was asking you about a proposal submitted to the Federal Assembly by four republics and two provinces on the constitution. So this was a proposal submitted to the Federal Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember that never came up before the Federal Assembly. I say that a proposal was submitted. I say it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, that can easily be established. There are documents about that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it quite clear already in 1990 that Slovenia had started with the secession, followed by Croatia, and that armies started to be formed in Slovenia and Croatia? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't put it that way. In Slovenia, yes. In Croatia, no, as far as I know. That's one thing. And secondly, this was part of the evolution of mutual relationships, relationships within which you were already manifesting a tendency to rule the whole country. And this was clear, among other things, from the way you crashed into the monetary system. You blocked goods coming from Slovenia. You organised people to hold public rallies in Ljubljana. So in a sense, you participated in the decisions made by Slovenia. You forced their hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the fact that a group of people from Kosovo wanted to go to Ljubljana to seek solidarity from the people of Slovenia with their suffering was not organised by Serbia, and you know that very well. And the fact that relations between the republican banks and the central banks was certainly not within the competence of the president of the Presidency of the republic but was within the competence of the national banks. And you're highly sensitive when you're attributed competencies that do not belong to you, but you are not so sensitive when you attribute everything else to someone else.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could prevent the purchase of goods by Serbian companies in Slovenia? No bank could do that. No administrative decision of Serbia was taken. This was a kind of civil revolt because of their attitude towards Kosovo and because of the way they treated the sufferers from Kosovo who wanted to address the Slovenian public to tell them the truth about their suffering and the persecution they were exposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying it was spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was partially spontaneous, but it certainly wasn't a state measure or a measure taken by the republic or any kind of administrative decision. It was simply generalised feelings of revolt because of such an attitude towards Kosovo. You know that very well. And why didn't you prevent the blockade of purchase of Slovenian goods?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, let's go back to the question of secession of Slovenia and Croatia in 1990. Is it true you were the federal Prime Minister in 1990? You were informed that already in mid-1990 a meeting was held between delegations of the HDZ and the Slovenian Demos, their ruling party at the time, to coordinate their tactics towards the JNA. You remember that? This was confirmed by Vasiljevic too, who in those days was head of the military security.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you received no information about that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any such information. I do know that in those days the HDZ, headed by Tudjman, had constituted its authority in Croatia, and as early as that date I don't think he could have done any such thing. He was the head of a party that was of no interest to me. What I was interested in was the work of state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that early in October 1990 there was intensified illegal arming of certain units in Croatia in cooperation with similar such institutions in Slovenia? And do you remember that the JNA discovered nine channels of illegal arming of Croatia and Slovenia in those days? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that there were some indications I received about arming in Slovenia. However, regarding arming in Croatia and what the army discovered by filming Spegelj and the import of Kalashnikovs and other weapons from Hungary, I learnt about it when it was broadcast on television. Even General Kadijevic never told me a word about it. And we asked him at a meeting why he hadn't informed the federal government of this. Since this was his duty as a military man, he should have informed the Presidency, but he should also have informed us so as to be kept informed. Not in the sense of us as commanders. But he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was in your term of office that the government of Croatia, in July 1990, decided to form the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time the decision was taken to withdraw the weapons of reserve police forces in areas where the majority Serb population which caused conflicts there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has its certain genesis, a course of development. Most of those weapons had already been handed over to the army, and the previous government in Croatia had done this. That is, the weapons of the so-called Territorial Defence. And all this had been handed to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were the Prime Minister when the Serbs were thrown out of the constitution of Croatia. What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to you who did not intervene to what the Serbs were doing in Croatia, I did intervene in response to what the Croats were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was your duty.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was your duty as well. I intervened by requesting a meeting in the Croatian Assembly at which I spoke about this at length. Among other things, I said what should be done to put an end to this. And I said quite clearly and listed things, starting from revanchism, the need to stop the army, to need to sit round a table and talk to the Serbs, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: What was your reaction when the Serbs were thrown out of the Croatian constitution? You were the president of the Presidency of Croatia for a time. You know the constitution of Croatia which defined Croatia as a state of the Croatian people, the Serb people, and others. What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reaction was that it was a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your reaction when the police raided Pakrac, Plitvice, or Borovo Selo and all the incidents that took place there? What was your reaction? You were the federal Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these things, via the army, was part of the competence of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. One could also ask what was the reaction was of the Federal Executive Council when the Serbs attacked Croatian villages, and there were such instances too. That was not in your competence so it was only within the competence of the Presidency and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pauses, please, between question and answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, the interpreters have really done remarkably well considering the difficulties they've had. Particularly with the witness and also the accused in particular taking up much room and time. Would you bear in mind -- we'll ask Mr. Markovic too, to pause, if he would, please. It's difficult, I know, because you're used to the language, but give the interpreters time. And you, Mr. Milosevic, you should also take time. You're not really allowing time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, please give me brief answers, because I have very little time. The agreement reached between the leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia regarding joint actions towards the JNA on the 20th of January, 1991, and before that on the 6th of January, 1991, the Defence Ministers met in Otocac to agree on coordinated action towards the JNA. Do you remember that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember that the army or, rather, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the General Staff was preparing an attack on the leadership of Croatia and Slovenia. That I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that the army carried out any attack.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't carry out an attack, but they were preparing it. I said that clearly and wrote that in my report for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that Article 5 of the constitution of SFRY stipulated that the borders could not be changed without agreement of all the republics and provinces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Yugoslav People's Army was absolutely pro-Yugoslav in orientation?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on one's judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a certain period of time that was true. Maybe up until the end of 1990. After that, it became increasingly pro-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the JNA, which was multi-ethnic in those days and which had a multi-ethnic leadership, was on the verge of intervening militarily to preserve Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Against all those undermining the unity of Yugoslavia. That was my understanding. Well, you said that just now.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of 1990 onwards, the army was increasingly in the function of implementing pro-Serb policies. I won't ask you. You're qualifying things without answering my questions. Tell me, what did you do as the number one man in the government of Yugoslavia when there was illegal arming across customs borders? At least that was within your terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about them. I learnt about them when the army published it, and meetings of the Presidency were held and instructions were given to the federal government. The federal government responded to the Presidency, and there was a session held sometime end of January 1991 when this was discussed for the first time in -- and what the powers of the Federal Executive Council are are clear. Even when you crashed into the monetary fund and took 18.2 billion dinars from it, we had no instruments that we could use against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not true, but I can't keep going back a hundred times to what you call the monetary incursion. Do you remember that in that atmosphere and under pressure of the European Community Stipe Mesic, who had already declared himself as a separatist, was elected president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic was due to be automatically elected president of the Presidency because that is what was stipulated by the constitution. That is the system of rotation for the President of the Presidencies. You prevented Mesic's election to the position of president of the Presidency, and for 45 days the Presidency did not have a president, which meant that the army was without a Commander-in-Chief for 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, when you say "you", I don't know who you mean, but by secret ballot, members of the Presidency did not wish to elect him because he himself clearly stated his intention to be the last president of Yugoslavia and that Yugoslavia should be dismembered.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right or not? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You must give the witness a chance to explain something. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that the Presidency was composed of eight members. Four members were either completely Serbian; that's Serbia, Vojvodina, or Kosovo, or Montenegro. They were hand-in-hand. They had identical positions. They were always able to outvote everybody. You always voted in unison, because Mesic was alone. The vote was 4 to 3. But the election of the president was never voted on. It was supposed to run automatically under the constitution. Mesic should have taken over from Jovic, just as Jovic in his time had taken over from Drnovsek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I asked you, was it true that even before he became a candidate for the President of the Presidency Mesic made it abundantly clear that he wanted to be the last president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and his latest statements on the break-up of Yugoslavia are also notorious. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter is not in dispute. The first thing you said is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You warned against the danger of civil war. You spoke in the Croatian Sabor or Assembly. That's true but that was only in June, 24th of June, 1991. Is that so, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the date here. It was on the 24th of June. It was broadcast live from the Croatian Assembly. And you knew full well that arming had been taking place in Croatia as early as 1990. Conflicts were in preparation in territories where Serbs were in jeopardy. How come that your reaction was so belated? It came only in mid-1991 when you spoke in the Croatian parliament of this danger.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably I have again to give my standard answer to explain this. My first meeting with Tudjman took place in Zagreb because my family resided in Zagreb. I worked in Belgrade, and I came to visit them over the weekend. And on one such occasion I asked to meet with him. We had never met before. And he asked me if I could stay on in Zagreb until Monday. I said I couldn't, so we met on a Sunday evening in Zagreb. I will not describe the circumstances to save time. My conclusion was that we could cooperate, one, if we can do without tit for tat and without retribution. That's one. Second, if we have negotiations with Serbs in Croatia and reach agreement with them. Another conclusion was to keep hands off Bosnia and Herzegovina, refrain from arming, et cetera. Even at that time, those were my demands from them. I repeated them many times in meetings with them. Before that decision was made back in the spring 1991 I demanded from the Assembly of Slovenia, the parliament of Croatia and the parliament of Serbia permission to address them on this subject, even though that was not my job strictly, formally, and legally speaking. And when I was allowed to address these parliaments, I did. In Serbia, I was never even allowed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no need -- there was no problem for you to address the Assembly of Serbia. Anybody who wanted to could have done so. Tell me another thing. Is it true that many garrisons were in dire straits at the time and were waiting for the JNA to save them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as soon as the government changed in Croatia Serbs, as an entity, were deleted from the Croatian constitution as a constituent nation and their situation deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I never agreed with that, and I didn't have the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, but is it true that Serbs had a good reason to be afraid?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that Serbs lived together with Croats, among Croats, that they were victims of mistreatment, and that they could hope for no justice from the current courts and the judiciary whose attitude was discriminatory?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, you are now making conclusions from something that is already history. We can now talk about something else, why talks were not held the way they should have been with Serbs in Croatia, not via Serbs in Serbia and through you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We sought to have direct negotiations between Knin and Zagreb, and we worked as mediators. But we will have opportunity later to see evidence of that. You say in paragraph 15 that I told you that we could not leave Serbs without protection. I suppose that it was clear even to you that they were undefended and unprotected in Croatia. Now, I as the president of Serbia am asking you, federal Prime Minister, and telling you that people should not be left in the lurch, unprotected, isn't it clearly your duty to take care of it? What's so strange about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was elected federal Prime Minister not as a Croatian but as a human being, and that's how I tried to act the whole time. Therefore, you cannot put it that way that I was supposed to react as a Croat. I was supposed to act as the president of a Yugoslav institution, which I was. I emphasised more than once that I had absolutely no powers, nor did the federal government, over the army, nor could we intervene in that sense. We made various proposals. We even sent our people there, various government cabinet members went. The vice-Prime Minister, including Markovic, et cetera. But they tried to deal with problems of turnover of goods, communications, normal supply of commodities to citizens, normal management of social affairs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Leave alone transactions and normal operations. You say in another item: "The republics arrogated to themselves revenues from various goods that they were supposed to pay into the federal budget."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that various republics stopped payments to the federal budget that were due?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that Slovenia did not pay its dues to the federal budget, and it stopped paying even the revenues that came from levies, customs levies that were charged at the borders that belonged to Slovenia. That much is true. But at that session I said that Croatia is paying its dues. Then Greguric took the floor and said that they would not be paying contributions to the army which is waging war on their territory. Macedonia did pay contributions. Bosnia and Herzegovina did too, but Serbia didn't. Look at the record of that session and you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assert that Serbia paid its contributions to the budget and demands were made in view of increased costs of the army resulting from failed contributions from other republics. Demands were made for Serbia to stop paying too.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. And if I could get the document, I could show it to you. And at that session which you quoted from several times, it is written very clearly what I said. I enumerated all those who were paying and who were not paying, and I said Serbia was among those who were not paying. You can find that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course we can find it. And you can get it. We were talking about financial institutions. You mentioned this Bank for International Economic Cooperation, JUBMES, and you spoke about Ivan Stambolic. You know very well, Mr. Markovic, at the time when he was appointed to that office, he was appointed at my request. In other words, he begged me to give him that post. And I achieved that in agreement with Branko Mikulic, then Prime Minister, not with you. Branko Mikulic, the Prime Minister before you, was in charge and he was able to do that because he was a candidate from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you ever ask me to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember. But it is possible that I asked you, too, to support his nomination, although it was not done, as you say, so that he should be removed from Serbia. He had already been removed from Serbia anyway. The truth is that at his request, I agreed with Branko Mikulic that he get that office. Do you admit that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I briefly describe our conversation on the phone on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can describe whatever you want. But the fact is that at that time, Branko Mikulic was Prime Minister, not you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There seems to be some difficulty with this particular microphone because that is supposed to cut the accused off so he doesn't take up so much time. Now, Mr. Markovic, if you want to respond, of course you should be able to and to describe the situation. You shouldn't be harried in any way by the accused in what you're trying to do. Now, if you would like to answer, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish to say, and I remember this very well, at that time I got a call from Mr. Milosevic, who asked me kindly if I could arrange that Mr. Ivan Stambolic be appointed somewhere outside Serbia, because for various reasons it was not good for him to stay in Serbia, both for his sake and for our sake. And he asked me if we could talk to Mr. Ilija Marjanovic, who was director general of the JUBMES, Yugoslav Bank for International Economic Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was just a candidate, a nominee.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was general director. He asked me, therefore, if we could talk to him and ask him to cede his position to Stambolic. I did call Stambolic. I explained to him the situation. Sorry, I called the general director and explained to him the situation and asked him to accept that he be replaced by Stambolic. That indeed happened. Stambolic was made general director and the previous director became his deputy. That was not the end of the matter, because after that Ivan Stambolic, who had not done this work before, had done his homework and did very well, he gave a great contribution to the development of this Bank for International Economic Cooperation until the time when his term of office was expiring. He -- Mr. Milosevic then talked to me again tete-a-tete and asked me to not support Stambolic's re-election. I refused, and I wrote a letter instead to the federal government suggesting -- excuse me. He wrote a letter to the federal government asking the federal government to withdraw their support for the re-election of Mr. Stambolic. I did not agree with this letter. And there were two cabinet members who were in favour of this letter, although they were his personal friends. I went to the Assembly instead and expressed my support to Stambolic. After that, Mr. Milosevic stopped all communication with the federal government and with me personally as its Prime Minister for several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it's matter with the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I brought this to an end because it is time for an adjournment, and the witness should certainly have one. You have, Mr. Milosevic, 25 minutes to conclude your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Tapuskovic is going to refer to -- I know Mr. Tapuskovic is going to refer to Exhibit 328, tab 16. At least, I think he is. The accused has been asking the witness questions about it. We've found the document. It's very extensive. There is in fact an English translation. I've marked the tabs with which I believe the passages the accused has asked him about. If the witness wants to see it at the break may he have it, to save time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness wants to see them, he may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have one minute private session? Nothing to do with the witness, just ongoing administrative matters but preferably now rather than to squeeze in at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you heard that I have been given only 25 minutes more, so please give me brief answers to my questions because I have a considerable number of questions left for you. But let us finish with Ivan Stambolic. I presume that it is not in dispute that he became president of the Yugoslav Bank for International Economic relations in 1987 at my intervention. I said that I intervened with the then-Prime Minister Branko Mikulic, and you say that I intervened with you too, or perhaps with you too. But anyway, is it in dispute that he was appointed at my intervention?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was appointed upon my intervention. Now, do you know, since you were friends, as you say, that he remained in that position until 1998, until he retired?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, but it is also well known that you asked me to have him dismissed from that position and that you wrote an official letter to the Federal Executive Council that his reappointment not be supported but to look for another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know about these personnel, current personnel matters from 1991, but isn't it clear that he remained in that position until 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not thanks to you. It was thanks to me. I went to the bank Assembly, and I on behalf of the Federal Executive Council and in my own name supported his reappointment and he got a large number of votes during that re-election. As a matter of fact, a large number of Serbian votes were in his favour, although these people had been instructed not to vote for him. And some people even left the building so as not to be in a position to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in 1987, he was not appointed at your initiative.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I cannot talk about this time when I was not Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He certainly did not remain until 1998. The remaining seven years at your initiative.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained for another four years when he was re-appointed upon my initiative and against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. And then again he remained until 1998.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, what does this have to do with anything, Ivan Stambolic with the war in Croatia, with the war in Bosnia, with the war in Kosovo and so on and so forth? And this is why you came to testify here. Was it this other side that instructed you to speak about this or are you doing this on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview in respect of these questions that are related to you, the question of Ivan Stambolic was brought up, and I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you ever so much. So this other side is interfering in matters that are of no concern to them. They won't let me be involved in the elections in Serbia and now they ask you about Ivan Stambolic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... by the accused, and tolerant though I am, I'm not going to put up with that. This was a proper range of inquiry with this witness, and he answered the questions that were raised with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to other matters then. I have here before me a newspaper from Croatia. Let me just look at the exact date. Feral Tribune is the newspaper. The 8th of November, 2003. It has to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. What is the relevance of this? The Prosecution are quite entitled to object to this -- just a moment. It's just the sort of objections that you have been raising. What is this before we get any sort of question about something as recent as that. He's dealing with matters ten years ago. That's the evidence that he's giving.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm dealing with the next topic, Mr. May, the one that the witness spoke about during his examination-in-chief when he said that he was endangered in Belgrade, that his life was in danger, that he slept with a gun underneath his pillow. So I have here an interview with Suvar, a Croatian politician, who also held an office in Belgrade at that time, and he says: "Before that, I also lived in Belgrade, and I was subjected to various accusations and threats and also when Ante Markovic, together with Slobodan Milosevic and Veljko Kadijevic, was breaking bread when the Serbian constitution was being adopted. I did not feel physically endangered. Therefore, I do not believe that Ante Markovic's live was physically in danger."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Stipe Suvar did not feel physically endangered and you lived in the residence of the federal Prime Minister in front of which there is police in uniform and you claim that you felt physically endangered in Belgrade. Can you say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give a response to that at all, because what makes some Stipe Suvar competent to deal with what I lived through? First of all, Stipe Suvar at that time was not in Belgrade. He had left Belgrade much earlier. So he absolutely could not have known anything about that. How I lived then I know the best. From the house where I lived, over the last several months of my life there, I did not take the same streets going to work. And as for people guarding me, many people were killed by persons who guarded them, precisely by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not openly talking about Yugoslavia. I'm just saying that so many people anywhere in the world were assassinated by people who were supposed to guard them and protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Belgrade 1989, 1990, 1991 when you feared for your own life? Who was killed then?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not talk about 1989 or 1990 or 1991. I was talking about the last few months of my stay in Belgrade, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a single example of anyone threatening your life in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. They organised demonstrations against me, and people were there against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, demonstrations. The other thing that Suvar speaks of here is this alleged missile that was fired at Banski Dvori. He says: "In Banski Dvori no one ever saw a crater or took a picture of one. It was a generally known fact that this had been rigged and that nobody targeted Banski Dvori, let alone JNA aircraft." And he says, "On the basis of everything that could be heard or read until now, it shows that a JNA aircraft that had taken off from Bihac had fired at Martin Spegelj's residence at Tuskanac." At his residence there. He was then minister of defence. This missile had fallen on Dubravkin Put but at Banski Dvori nobody saw a crater or took a picture of one. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, now I could say that I'm not interested in entering a debate with Mr. Stipe Suvar. He is absolutely in no position to say anything about this. He had no access there. He could have invented anything, that Americans had come and done the bombing. What I can say here has nothing to do with Stipe Suvar. I'm not interested in him at all. But what I can say is the following: That I was in Zagreb between the 5th and 10th of October. The reason was purely personal. My first grandson was born then, and I was trying to find a way of getting to Zagreb. At that time, all the communications between Belgrade and Zagreb had been severed, so I travelled via Austria. When I arrived in Zagreb, Tudjman called me and asked for a meeting. He had found out that I was there. He wanted to talk to me about the initiative to have this moratorium, and during that period relations in Yugoslavia, in the former Yugoslavia, were supposed to be worked out without any bloodshed, and he wanted to discuss this with me, and he was trying to tell me that I should speak to Stipe Mesic so that he would return to Belgrade. So the three of us, Mr. Tudjman, Stipe Mesic, and I had a meeting and discussed this. And we had agreed about certain matters that Stipe Mesic should return to Belgrade, that the ministers and I should return to Belgrade, and also we agreed that people who were in the Federal Assembly, some of them should also return to Belgrade. Then we also agreed that Kucan should be called. Tudjman lifted the receiver wanting to call Kucan, and at that moment the missiles exploded. I was actually present, I was there at the place where the missiles exploded. One of these missiles exploded precisely in the dining room where perhaps a minute or half a minute before that we had been having lunch. And there were craters there. And the door was torn down and the staircase. And we tried to get out in all conceivable ways. In other areas that are close to this building, there were other craters, all the way to Dubravkin Put. So that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In Hrvatska Ljevica, October 2003, this is a newspaper also, it says in connection with you, "Perhaps he will say something about the rigged explosion in Banski Dvori when he had talks with Tudjman. We can say with full reliability that Banski Dvori had not been attacked. Any military expert who wanted to do so could have done so at the time. For example, it can be seen quite clearly in the photograph that the chandelier in Tudjman's study --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. We will see whether the witness can give any evidence at all about this newspaper report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about these newspaper reports, who wrote them, and who is competent to write them. Mr. Milosevic is using materials that are totally incompetent. The fact remains that missiles were fired, seven or eight of them, and one man was even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was this man killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These missiles hit the building that we were in, two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was somebody killed in that building?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then on the other side facing a street called Visoka and two were down there in Dubravkin Put, the street of Dubravkin Put. So that is what I can say in this regard. One really had to live through this kind of thing in order to know what it was like. And now that I should debate the issue with people that I don't know at all who could have written anything about this, that is pointless, absolutely pointless. The fact remains that General Tus, who had been a pilot for years himself, and he was commander of the Yugoslav air force, it was his assessment that these missiles were fired from a particular aircraft and from a particular altitude, and this could have been done only by three pilots in Yugoslavia. I think that General Tus is an expert in these matters as opposed to others who write about it this way or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to read the last sentence out to you, and it says: "Perhaps Markovic himself simply did not know about the trick that was supposed to be performed before the Yugoslav and foreign public." Because nobody got killed in Banski Dvori; isn't that right? The missiles were fired and nobody got killed. Is that right, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The missiles were fired, but there were some who had been injured. I cannot say who exactly. I know that one man got killed. I know that for sure, and I know that others were injured. It was not my job to deal with that. I had been bombed. And on the other hand, I don't believe that it would be credible for Tudjman to have bombed himself. I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there was no bombing or shelling of Banski Dvori as you say. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not competent to engage in this kind of debate. It would have to be somebody else. And I think that the person who wrote this is certainly not competent. Anything can be written on paper. I'm surprised that Mr. Milosevic uses such arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have Croatian newspapers here.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do newspapers mean? All sorts of things are written in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're right about that. All sorts of things are written in newspapers. And is it also true, the other thing they say here, it is interesting that perhaps the greatest support enjoyed by Mr. Markovic was among the JNA General Staff, and it is also said that when Kadijevic, towards the end of 1990, suggested that after the military coup you as the legally elected Prime Minister should take over the position of president of the country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so on this very same page there are some things that are written that are correct and others that are not correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is because this was copied from what I said myself. Until then, nobody had known about this except for Kadijevic and myself. And if somebody wrote about this, they wrote about it only on the basis of what I said right here, and that is the truth, that Kadijevic did come to me with a plan that had been elaborated in the General Staff to arrest the leaderships of Croatia and Serbia and that this should be done separately from the Presidency, and then the Presidency, since it had been sidestepped, would be replaced and somebody would have to take over that function. And when I said, "Where does Milosevic fall within all of this and everybody else?" He jumped to his feet and said, "He is the only one who is struggling for Yugoslavia and he is the only one who supports this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm the only one who is struggling for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you're the only one who supports the arrest of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so why did he not arrest them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he had not have any political back-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I did not back him up politically either. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he could have if he wanted to. Mr. Markovic, rather, could have if he wanted to. Mr. Markovic was supposed to be your weapon, your tool, yes, your tool, your weapon, Mr. Kadijevic's tool, Mr. Kadijevic's weapon in order to arrest these two leaderships.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that we were not on good terms and then you were supposed to be my weapon?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was on bad terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You and I.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I was just supposed to be used as your weapon, your tool, so that you would rule over all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right, Mr. Markovic. Very interesting. Most interesting construction. Now, tell me please, since I quoted this report of Suvar's, there is a question that he himself raises here and that I would like to put to you. You claim that Tudjman and I agreed in Karadjordjevo on splitting up Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to claim. Both of you confirmed that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not true that I ever confirmed this to you. Now, whether Tudjman ever said something like that to you, that's different. Do you know that stenographic notes were presented here from Tudjman's meeting with his closest collaborators, and they commented upon (redacted) , saying that this is a blatant falsehood. That's what he said to his closest collaborators. How do you think he would tell you something different, something that he did not even tell his closest collaborators?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go into who said things to other people. What I wrote down in my private notes was about a meeting with Mr. Tudjman and with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic about Karadjordjevo and the split-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely false. Now, what Tudjman could have said to you, I don't believe that. After all, we denied it in public, but I certainly never told you any such thing. This is what Stipe Suvar says, because the journalist put the following question to him: "Milosevic and Tudjman allegedly confirmed to Markovic that they had agreed on splitting up Bosnia." And he answers: "All right. But Markovic did not have to wait for 12 years in order to tell us about this." If this had really been the truth, why did you wait for 12 years in order to tell the story that Tudjman and I had reached agreement or that Tudjman and I had said to you that we had reached such agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor asked me to appear here in this court, then I said everything I knew. Before that, I did not speak up. I spoke up because the court in The Hague asked me to be a witness here, and that is when I spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The hearing is due to come to a halt fairly soon. There is five minutes left for you, Mr. Milosevic. Then We will divide the time, the last half hour, between the remaining parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry. I mean, during five minutes. Well, anyway, this is completely false, this about the split-up of Bosnia. And after all, there are stenographic notes of Tudjman's confidential talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned, as far as I could see from your statement, you say that there were two items on the agenda of the meeting between Tudjman and myself. You say one was the split-up of Bosnia and the other one was the dismissal of Ante Markovic. Doesn't it seem to you that - how should I put this? - that you are attaching too much importance to yourself, that we are discussing your dismissal? What do I care about your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss it. You both attached this importance to me, and you said to me, Mr. Milosevic, that this was a proposal made by Mr. Tudjman, not myself, and I did not have any reason to disagree with it. As a matter of fact, you said that you gave it a certain deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I was told that this was your proposal but that it would be postponed for a while. So see, I even remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I remember the details too.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You suffer from amnesia now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Markovic, I never suffer from amnesia, but since you on certain occasions used Boro Jovic's book, then perhaps you can find that in the book too. Since your dismissal was Tudjman's issue, not mine. It's not that I think that he raised it but simply he was head of Croatia, and you were an appointee from Croatia. So it was not for me to --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, but it was not for Tudjman to say anything. I was not elected according to any kind of republican criterion to head the federal government. That was the only position that did not fall within that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. Every time an effort was made to get a Prime Minister from a different republic. And there is also an anecdote that Tudjman said to me, of course not in Karadjordjevo, because in Karadjordjevo no one thought of mentioning you at all. When I asked him what job he'd give Ante Markovic, he said since he is an electrician I'm going to let him to fix fuses. So that is what Borovic wrote down in his diary. I suppose you remember that too?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A different official from Croatia during the elections in Croatia in 1990, his name is Djodan, and there is a text to that effect. That's what he said. He said: "Ante Markovic should not delve into politics. He is an electrical engineer. Let him fix fuses."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Markovic. Is it correct that you established a political party of reformists, but it was only after the multi-party elections in Croatia were held?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I established it when I could establish it on the basis of Yugoslavia law. Before that, I could not have established it. The Yugoslav law was passed in the month of June 1990, and it was only after that that I could have done this. In the proposals that were presented by the Federal Executive Council towards the end of 1989, I proposed a change of the constitution which would make it possible to have multi-party elections held throughout Yugoslavia. Since this was not the case, then I could not have any elections either in Croatia or in Slovenia because they held their elections before this law was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, but your party of reformists did take part in the elections in Serbia and in the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the elections in other republics. I assume that this is not a fact you're going to deny.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. On the contrary, of course I participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you suffered a total loss in all these elections.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true either. It wasn't a total loss. It was a partial loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if there are 29 seats in the Macedonian Assembly, then that is not total defeat, or if there is a number of MPs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then that is not a loss either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many MPs did you have in the Assembly of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were very popular and that we were jealous of you because you were so popular in Serbia. How come you did not win a single seat in the Serbian parliament?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was the way I was, as you had put it, you made it impossible to have elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did take part in elections in Serbia. These were the first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but elections were allowed only after the law was passed towards the end of June 1990. I think it was the 25th of June or something like that. It was only after that that this was possible. Before that, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That only confirms that we in Serbia did hold multi-party elections in accordance with the law and after we had changed the constitution and after we introduced a multi-party system.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you took part in the elections in accordance with federal law and the constitution of Serbia that had been changed.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part. It was people from Serbia who took part, those who organised the alliance of reformist forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Markovic, tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is bringing your examination to an end. You have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Markovic. Since you talked about some kind of major reform programme of yours, is it correct that you explained that there was a great deal of foreign currency around, according to your very well known, unrealistic exchange rate, a lot of foreign currency was sold, and that is how you destroyed the foreign exchange reserves totally.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Those like you destroyed them, those who robbed the National Bank of Yugoslavia, who robbed 18.2 billion dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't foreign exchange.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had dinars could buy foreign exchange, and you know that full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you exaggerated the foreign exchange reserves and then when the so-called succession was discussed, then these so-called foreign exchange reserves were sought from Serbia and Montenegro? And since there weren't any, then what was divided was the gold that Serbia and Montenegro had brought into the first Yugoslavia. You as former Prime Minister should be aware of these facts.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the National Bank of Yugoslavia controlled the foreign exchange reserves. It wasn't done by the government. And these reports are reports that were presented either in the public or for internal use by the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time -- the time is up. Yes. We will have to divide the time, as I say, between the amicus and the Prosecution. So they've each got about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the great host of facts covered in the summary, I would like to ask if we could link -- clarify some matters linked to paragraph 45 regarding para armies and paragraphs 37, 38 and 39. And I will focus on these matters only, these being matters that have not been touched upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to begin with paragraphs 37, 38, and 39. Mr. Markovic, I will let you see everything I refer to. This is an exhibit that was admitted through Mr. Mesic. We mentioned the number today. It is Exhibit 328, tab 16. And I have a copy in B/C/S, and I have highlighted the passages I intend to refer to. Could you please look first at page 74. Page 74, please. In the English version it is page 62, paragraph 3. Of the English version, page 62, paragraph 3. I say this for the benefit of Their Honours and the Prosecution. Have you found it? It's highlighted.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
