utterances.text: You said this today: "As regards the competence and functioning, I've already noted it is a fact that the Presidency, after the 15th of May, up until the 1st of July when it was constituted with the help of the Troika, it was not functioning. It didn't function during a time period in which some dramatic events happened for the fate of the country." Is that right? You said that today?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And on page 75, last paragraph, please. You said -- this is page 63 of the English version. "The Presidency must be in session continuously, just as the Federal Executive Council. There isn't a day doesn't go by without us meeting, because every day some new developments occur and we need to consult." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they don't have this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I refer to certain things that were common knowledge, can I ask you, were you following those events between the 24th and the 27th of June, which were critical, and did you know that Croatia had declared its independence on the 25th as had the Assembly of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that Slovenia had decided to take over all functions of the federation on the state border towards Austria, Italy, Hungary and also to establish a state border towards the rest of Yugoslavia, which means towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on that day Slovenia implemented that decision that very day?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I'm not quite sure whether it could have done everything in one day, but in principle, those were the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Assembly of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the absence of delegates from Slovenia and Croatia, did it conclude that both decisions of Slovenia and Croatia were unconstitutional asking the appropriate federal authorities to restore things to normal?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you as the Federal Executive Council take any decision or order on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What day? What do you mean? On what page is this referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you took two decisions on that day. Mr. Markovic, I do not -- I'm not in a position to conduct my own investigation, but I have a book by Janez Jansa, Slovenian Defence Minister in those days, and both of these two decisions are published in the book. I have photocopies of those decisions. If you could look at the book and the photocopies of these decisions, could you confirm whether those are the decisions that you took, though they're not signed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Show them to me and I'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you are. They're not lengthy. One is one page long and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other half a page long. Are those the decisions that you signed? They're not signed in this copy.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision that we took and signed, and this order, I don't recollect it being drafted or signed by me. The order was not signed by me. That I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that this order --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember the decision, and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this order, it says --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The order on the prohibition of establishing frontier crossings.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, and I said I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that it says, "The federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs and the federal Secretariat for National Defence will implement this decision."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I don't remember the decision, I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember on the basis of the book written by the Defence Minister of Slovenia Janez Jansa --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read that book and I don't have time for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But my question is do you know on the 22nd of June a meeting was held between Tudjman and Kucan and the top leadership of both republics on taking over borders immediately following the proclamation of independence? And when complete agreement was not reached, then Tudjman and Kucan agreed at least not to allow the army to pass through the area which the Slovenian forces would take control of.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that meeting or that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this decision that you admit you signed was taken on the 26th in the morning, about 4.00 a.m.? Did you take that decision about 4.00 a.m. -- 4.00 a.m. on the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of June the decision was taken. That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And not on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it's not signed. Let me draw your attention to what he said in the book, and I'm asking you whether it is correct. "On the 26th of June at 11.10 in our information centre a fax arrived from Joze Slokar --" who was a member of the Federal Executive Council at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "-- for Milan Kucan in which he sent us the gist of two decisions adopted by the federal government during a night meeting that went on until 3.30. We had the official military order on our table." Is it true that the decision was taken early in the morning on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. The session was held on the 25th, and anyway, I don't know why that is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Because in this statement that you gave to the Prosecution, in paragraph 37, you said that you spoke with Kucan on the 26th of June in the morning, and it was that morning that you took the decision, and the military action started the following night, so you couldn't have spoken to him the next day, the 27th. And that is what Jansa says too.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, now whether it is one day or the other, in any event, it is a fact which has not been denied by Kucan either, and it has been registered. I wanted it to be registered, the fact that he called me early in the morning at 4.00 a.m. -- three minutes past four, and that he spoke about this. And I noted that the attack took place on the 26th. It may have been the 27th, I can't guarantee that 100 per cent, but it is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is very important, because on the 26th, there were no conflicts in the territory of Slovenia, only the following night.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, then, maybe the next night, if that's what you say. I would have to review all my documents to be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if it says in that order that you were supposed --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I do not recollect any such order being issued. You're taking me back to the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But look what it says in this decision.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I read it. You don't need to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I have to. In point 3, it says -- and this is what you signed -- "If at the frontier crossing physical or any other kind of resistance is put up or such resistance can be expected, officers of the federal Secretariat are duty-bound to assist them upon their request." Does that mean resort to force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Secretariat for National Defence. No, for internal affairs and not national defence. The -- this refers to the police, because in the previous paragraph it says: "The federal Secretariat for the interior hitherto the Federal Secretariat." So if you read that carefully, you should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I've seen that. But my question is: Who opened fire first? Was the order first issued by the command of the Territorial Defence to fire at the soldiers when soldiers were killed or were there any victims among the civilians? Who was the first to open fire during the events on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is hard to say. But judging by what reached me, the army came out of the barracks, started marching with tanks and cannon across Slovenia. That is what I learnt from Milan Kucan, and that is what General Kadijevic later confirmed when I asked him. When I asked him at the federal government meeting, "Who gave you permission for this." He said, "No one. We acted on our own."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in paragraph 38, somewhere halfway, you said the following: "The military intervention in Slovenia was carried out with the agreement of Borisav Jovic," who was, of course, Milosevic's man. This is an order that you signed of your own free will. Nobody forced you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is not an order to use the army in Slovenia. It's something quite different. The reference here is only to the border, the function of the police on the border and of frontier units on the border. I don't have evidence in my hands that Jovic issued such an order, but conversations between him and me showed that he was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm afraid your time is coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do appeal to you to give me a few more minutes. I promise not to take more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid the time has had to go to the accused first of all. I'm afraid we have to give the others time to fit in, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this would be very useful. It is -- it relates to paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to put something in writing to us, yes, but time has really run out on everybody. We had to try and do the fairest we can. We said 15 minutes, and that's the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a key to the problems that arose at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, much has been built by the accused on your role in Slovenia, not a matter on which evidence was focused in the examination-in-chief. The matter has been touched on in Exhibit 427, tab 6, which is somewhat unhappily photocopied. If the usher would be good enough to lay the English version on the overhead projector and to hand to you these pages, can we deal with this very swiftly. The material is in tab -- Exhibit 47 [sic], tab 6. It's hard to find, thus I've placed it on the overhead projector. Mr. Markovic, did you say, bottom of the page 2: "It is possible that the situation at the border was actually fine but we don't know that. What I want --" bottom of the page, please, Usher. "But what I want to say is that the institutions --" down a little bit, please. That's fine. Thank you. "What I want to say is that the institutions which have international obligations and are responsible for that cannot bear that responsibility." "Third, since it's been repeated over and over again regarding war between Federal Executive Council and Slovenia, I must say that this is an absolute lie because Federal Executive Council made no such decision, and as far as the decision that was made by the Federal Executive Council is concerned, the members of the Federal Executive Council from Slovenia took part in the decision-making, the same members who handed in their resignation now. The decision was made after Slovenia had taken over the borders by a unilateral act after it had taken over the customs by a unilateral act, as well as flight control also by a unilateral act with no consent. Federal Executive Council made a decision on direct securing of realisation of federal regulations on trespassing the state border in the territory of the republic..." And you went on to say, and I'm going to read this now in two paragraphs: "In order to secure execution of the federal regulations on trespassing the state border and movement in the border area in the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. And also in order to secure the execution of Yugoslavia international obligations and free traffic..." and right at the top, please: "... and movement of people over the state border, the federal Secretariat of the Interior will directly take over, that is secure realisation of controlling the passing of the state border. That means that the federal Secretariat was assigned this task. Second, while directly providing execution of federal regulations on trespassing the border, Secretariat of Interior will establish direct cooperation with JNA." Now, just very briefly, and preferably in a sentence or even a word, did that amount to your commanding the army or did it amount to your taking steps to secure the borders and seeking the cooperation of the army? But very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very clearly stated. Our conclusion was that the federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs needs to secure everything that relates to Yugoslavia's borders, and accordingly, the federal Secretariat was allowed to communicate with the federal Secretariat for National Defence so as to engage border JNA units, because this had to do with crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We only have ten more minutes. I must cut you short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm advised you will find in the 1974 constitution at paragraphs 158, 161, and 213 the limits of the power in respect of the army. His Honour Judge Robinson asked about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you've been asked a large number of questions about Slovenia and the suggestion has been put that you had something to do with the use of the army, I will have to expand the evidence in due course to be given by the military expert. Please help us with these three points: If evidence shows that the JNA on the 28th of June delivered cluster ammunition in an area of Slovenia, Trebnje, did you have anything to do with that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. Trebinje, after all, is a long way from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, there's a small town of Trebnje in Slovenia. Next question. If the 140th JNA unit left the Tito barracks on the 2nd of July, 1991, and fired on the Slovenian town of Gornje Vas, did you have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have anything to do with it? I had nothing to do with it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now please look at two intercepts very briefly. They've been produced. I'll hand them, for the overhead projector, on English versions with the B/C/S versions available for the witness. The first is Exhibit 613, tab 9. The underlying question is whether the accused had the intentions he implies, to keep Slovenia in federal Yugoslavia. The admissibility of this, as all intercepts, is pending. This one is the 17th of June. It's between Karadzic and Milosevic. And halfway down the first page, we see Karadzic speaking of Croatia and Slovenia. We then see Milosevic saying: "You see that they want to step out... They are carrying out these things exactly the way we planned it." "Yes, that is right." "Exactly the way we planned it," said the accused. Karadzic: "My only fear is that he --" and this is, I think, a reference to you -- "might get carte blanche from the army, i.e., the army might support him; if he imposed the measures, he would impose them symmetrically -- there where they should be -- where they should and there where they should not be imposed." I want you to look at the next one. Perhaps we can briefly look at the third page of this one, please, where it has, halfway down, the accused saying, "Well, I think that things are going exactly the way we predicted." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." "We will see how this Federation will --" Karadzic: "Yes, yes, that will be interesting. So you're meeting with Markovic tonight." If you could look at the next intercept and then I will ask for your comment. The next intercept is Exhibit 353, tab 28. We need only look at the bottom of the first page, having seen in the middle of the first page the topic of the conversation between Karadzic and the accused is Croatia and Slovenia. You can see that exactly in the middle of the screen now, but at the foot of the page, please, Usher, and right down to the bottom of the page. "That's clear," says the accused. "They should be allowed to separate." Karadzic: "Yes." Then over the page, please, Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Now there's only one question left, to have disintegration in line with our inclinations." About six lines down, the accused: "Well, they mustn't wait for him, no. Concerning Slovenia, I would let them go immediately." Karadzic: "Yes." The accused: "Let them go immediately and the others as well after they've settled the issues of borders with us," and then he deals with some other particular matter. Just help us, please, Mr. Markovic: Were you aware at the time of what the accused's genuine intention was in relation to retaining Slovenia and Croatia within the Federation or letting them go?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, as far as Slovenia was concerned, it was clear that they wanted to let Slovenia go. As for Croatia, as a part of the Serb people were there, I can't say that they were ready for it, but I did listen to a part of these telephone conversations between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic, that is true, and I fully recognise their voices. That was what they discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm wrong in the attribution of the number. This was 353, tab 30, I'm told. Alternatively, it's Exhibit 613, intercept 15, for the record. You've been asked questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may seek your indulgence. A great deal of matters have been raised and I have got a couple of points that may be of value to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked questions about the revenue. There is an exhibit in this case, Mr. Jovic's statement under 89(F), it's Exhibit 596, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher could place paragraph 45 on the overhead projector, please, for me. Bottom of the page. Thank you very much. Right at the bottom of the page, please, paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Evidence has been given to this effect: On the 8th of January, during a conversation with Radmilovic, Jovic criticised him for everything they were doing with the primary issues of money and with the revenues that belonged to the Federation. He explained without it they, the SPS, certainly would have lost the elections because more than half of the republic would not have received wages and pensions. He said that Ante - you - were surprised and flabbergasted that we were not bankrupt but we outwitted him. Milosevic was obviously avoiding informing me because I could not have justified that as president of the PSFRY. At the end of our conversation, Milosevic appeared and Stanko said please defend me against the criticism of the president of the SFRY Presidency. To that Milosevic responded, I will defend you for taking the money, but I will not defend you for proposing the adoption of laws and resolutions in order to carry this out. What do you say to the evidence that's been given by Jovic about the taking of the money? Accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stambolic and his appointment and dismissal, was that within the competence of the president of Serbia, as the accused was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused subsequently wanted Stambolic out of that office. Why did he want him out of that office?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted him replaced. He replaced him politically from the position of president of the Presidency of Serbia, and then he took care to appoint him somewhere else outside Serbia so that he wouldn't bother him. He wouldn't stand in his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... right at the end of the examination about Karadjordjevo, the meeting, and your discussion of that with the accused. The accused claimed to the Court that he had a full memory of the incident but declined to put that recollection of the meeting to you, turning instead to an observation about your training, your original training in electrical skills. So you haven't been challenged. Is your account of the Karadjordjevo meeting, the description of it by the accused, is it unchanged and unaffected by the evidence -- by the questions you've been asked? Do you stand by your original version, please? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have been asked questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what's your point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I stated quite clearly that it is absolutely untrue that there was any discussion in Karadjordjevo between Tudjman and me about the division of Bosnia and that it is absolutely untrue that I spoke about that with Ante Markovic, and that is what I said. Despite this, Mr. Nice says that I didn't challenge it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, two other points and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made the observation about Bogicevic being led on to vote in a certain way in a room that the army intimidated people in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a short clip from The Death of Yugoslavia film which is available. I don't know if the Chamber has seen the film generally. I'll just, with your leave, play this and see if this is the passage that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the session that was held. I didn't attend. None of us others attended, regardless of the position I held. And that is where pressure was brought to bear to take a decision to proclaim a state of emergency in the country, and such a state of emergency would give a free hand to the army. And that decision was not taken because Bogic Bogicevic, even though a Serb, he represented Bosnia and Herzegovina at the meeting, he voted against it. And Tupurkovski also, whom we see now, he voted against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time -- the clip lasts about seven minutes. I'm happy to make it available to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should say that it shows all the participants wearing their coats. It was indeed the cold exercise referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter of detail to correct the record, I suspect in my last question, Mr. Markovic: In speaking of Kadijevic's offer to you, you spoke of his plan to arrest the leadership of two states. Which two states -- the leadership of which two states did he propose arresting?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He proposed arresting Franjo Tudjman and his associates and Milan Kucan and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record at page 23 and at the time 13:03:32 speaks of Croatia and Serbia. I think that the witness misspoke rather than there being a misrecording by the stenographer, but he's now made it clear it's Slovenia and Croatia. I shan't seek your indulgence further. There is one other unrelated and private session matter that will take 30 seconds to deal with, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish his evidence because he's waited with patience for a rather long time. Mr. Markovic, we're going to release you. We'll come back to exhibits in a moment. We'll come back to any submissions, but we're going to allow the witness to go instead of having to wait here. As I say, Mr. Markovic, thank you for coming back and thank you for giving your evidence all today, but you are now concluded. You go with the thanks of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with the various matters which we need to do. We'll start with various items of exhibit we should deal with. We have two items which I think the accused has given us. Is there any objection to any of these? The Prosecution can have a look at them during the adjournment briefly and then hand them back. I don't anticipate there will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are the agendas. I've made the point. They appear to be originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. They can have the next exhibit number. D numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour the agenda for 1989 will be Defence Exhibit 223.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 224. And the agenda for 1990 will be 225, Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are these two documents. The first is the decision on immediate ensuring of implementation of federal regulations on the state borders on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia that Mr. Ante Markovic says he signed. This copy is unsigned, but it was submitted to the Slovenian side in that form. And the second, which he doesn't recall signing, is the order prohibiting the formation of frontier crossings within the territory of SFRY. Both documents are brief. One is a page and a half, the other half a page, and I believe that this could be marked for identification, translated, and probably used later on in an endeavour to get hold of the originals of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give that the next number for the Court, its own numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Court Exhibit 27, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, perhaps you omitted to mention, because in addition to these two exhibits, that is the agendas regarding Mirko Markovic's [as interpreted] activities for 1989, 1990, there are several other documents that have their ERN numbers and which I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. received from the side opposite when I challenge some of the statements of Mr. Markovic. So I have here part of the minutes, 01044526, for -- which has to do with General Kadijevic's reporting to Prime Minister Markovic in connection with Slovenia, losses, casualties, hotbeds, et cetera, in other words, about military issues. So I should like to tender that into evidence as well. And I also have a report by Kacic, 01075129, and I quoted this sentence: "If you can't talk to Jokic, you have here in The Hague Kadijevic and Prime Minister Markovic. With reference to Dubrovnik, he is placed in the most prominent position as someone who should intervene." And the third document is Jagar's statement, ERN number 01112475, which says how Ante Markovic is using two cards and that he will not leave Belgrade until he destroys Serbia and Milosevic. This is ERN number 01112478 which I'm tendering into evidence. And finally, the shorthand minutes from a session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia from which I quoted Markovic who speaks about the spontaneous, chaotic movements, out of control in all areas of life, saying that no one is able to control events any more, and again I quoted a member of the Presidency from Vojvodina, Jugoslav Kostic, who says he will not vote in favour of giving the army a free hand. It is a very lengthy report, but I've highlighted the parts, the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've got -- we've only got a limited time. There's no need to go over it again. What is the date of that final document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 12th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you hand those documents in first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I make two observations? First of all, the witness had to deal with these things without being given the documents to look at, and did deal with them. Secondly, we still haven't had a chance to review them for any purpose, really, and certainly not to see the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will ensure for the moment that -- the time is limited. We will mark them for identification, and we will try to make sure that none have in fact already been introduced, which they may have done. It may be simpler to deal with this over the time. Yes. One by one, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the minutes dealing with General Kadijevic is Defence Exhibit 226 marked for identification. The report is Defence Exhibit 227 marked for identification. Jagar's statement is Defence Exhibit 228 marked for identification; and the shorthand minutes of July 12, 1991, is Defence Exhibit 229 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the short extract from The Death of Yugoslavia be an exhibit? It's about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At some stage I think we must make a decision about this particular document. Have we -- have we not admitted it already?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it's not been admitted. It's been the subject of recurring discussion but it hasn't been formally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us the mark this part also as a Prosecution number, mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This particular part is, like so much of it, it is live footage of events interspersed with commentary. Curiously or interestingly, they actually photographed and filmed the actual meeting so you see the voting and the men cuddled up in their coats, but of course that comes with commentary in between from Mesic and Tupurkovski and people like that. But I don't see that as a principal objection. But if it can be marked certainly at this stage we'll review it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This section is seven minutes. The programme itself is three television programmes long. I think it's about three hours. And very interesting viewing, if I may so. With a great deal of contemporaneous, or more contemporaneous interviewing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And tomorrow, before we go into private session, what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tomorrow we'll continue with the private session witness first and conclude that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, provided that's the case, then that involves no problem about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- go on with the witness we've already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have another witness who has been served as an expert. There's some concern about the position of his evidence, but we're advised, and I understand that it is entirely expertise and there's room for one more witness should we reach him, a short witness, called Soldal at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The important thing is that we finish the witness we've already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that we do deal with any particular witness we have to deal with tomorrow or he will have to be prepared to come back the following Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope we can deal with him tomorrow. And then there's one short matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we'll do is we'll mark the part that was just played, the short part played today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit 635.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
